label: ex:twist given by $2$-cocycle
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:twist given by $2$-cocycle}
  Throughout 
  we will  refer back
  to the special case
  treated in \cite{DGNRW:Cartan} where the twist over $G$ is induced
  by a continuous 
  \emph{normalized $2$-cocycle}
  ${c}\colon G^{(2)} \to \mathbf{T}$, meaning that
  ${c}$ satisfies ${c}(g_{1},g_{2}){c}(g_{1}g_{2}, g_{3})={c}(g_{1},g_{2}g_{3}){c}(g_{2}, g_{3})$ for all $(g_{1},g_{2},g_{3})\in G^{(3)}$ and ${c}(g,s(g))=1={c}(r(g),g)$ for all $g\in G$. The associated twist
  $\mathcal{E}_{{c}}$ is defined as follows.
  As a set, 
  $\mathcal{E}_{{c}}$ is given by $G\times\mathbf{T}$, but the multiplication is
  twisted by the $2$-cocycle:
  $(g_{1},z_{1})\cdot(g_{2},z_{2}) =
  (g_{1}g_{2},{c}(g_{1},g_{2})z_{1}z_{2})$.
  In this case, we choose $\iota$ to be the inclusion map and $\pi$ to be the projection
  onto the first component.

label: rem-pedantry
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem-pedantry} The notation in \eqref{eq:2} is meant to ensure
  that the sum is interpreted as being over the countable set
  $G^{r(e')}$ and not over the uncountable set~$\mathcal{E}^{r(e')}$.  A more
  pedantic approach would be to introduce any set-theoretic section
  $\mathfrak{s}\colon G\to\mathcal{E}$ for $\pi$ and write
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:3}
    f_{1}*f_{2}(e') =\sum_{g\in G^{r(e')}} f_{1}(\mathfrak{s}(g))f_{2}(\mathfrak{s}(g)^{-1} e'),
  \end{equation}
  and to observe that the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:3} does not
  depend on the choice of section.  In the spirit of Winston
  Churchill's reaction to allegedly misplaced prepositions, we have
  chosen to write \eqref{eq:2} in place of \eqref{eq:3} to keep our
  formulas less daunting.  It also helps us connect to more general
  treatments, where $G$ is not necessarily {\'e}tale, such as
  \cite{MW:1992:CtsTrace} where the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:2} is
  simply the integral of the function $\pi(e)\mapsto f_{1}(e)f_{2}(e^{-1} e')$
  with respect to counting measure on $G^{r(e')}$.

label: lem:Urysohn
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Urysohn}
    Suppose $\mathcal{E}$ is a twist over a  locally compact, Hausdorff\ {\'e}tale\ groupoid~$G$. For any $e_0\in \mathcal{E}$, there exists an element $f\in C_{c}(G;\mathcal{E})$ such that $f(e_0)\neq 0$ and $\pi(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f))$ is a bisection.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Tietze's extension theorem, we may find $g_0\in C_c(\mathcal{E})$ such
  that $g_0(z\cdot e_0)=z$; the function
  $g\colon e\mapsto \int_\mathbf{T} z g_0(\bar z\cdot e)\,\mathrm{d}z$ is then in
  $C_c(G;\mathcal{E})$ and satisfies $g(e_0)=1$.  Since $G$ is {\'e}tale, it
  has a basis of open bisections
  \cite{Renault:gpd-approach}*{Proposition~I.2.8}, so by Urysohn's, we
  can find a $q\in C_{c}(G)$ such that $\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(q)$ is a bisection of
  $G$ with $\pi(e_0) \in \operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(q)$; in particular, $f\colon e\mapsto q(\pi(e))g(e)$ is an element of $C_{c}(G;\mathcal{E})$ such that $f(e_0)\neq 0$ and $\pi(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f))$ is a bisection.

label: ex-abelian
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex-abelian} Suppose that $\mathcal{E}$ is a twist over an {\'e}tale\
  groupoid $G$ and that $\mathcal{E}$ is a bundle of abelian groups.  That is,
  we assume that $\mathcal{E}$ is an abelian twist.  Of course, this implies
  that $G$ is abelian as well.  Then $C_{c}(G;\mathcal{E})$ is commutative.
  Hence $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$ is commutative.


  Conversely, if $\mathcal{E}$ is not a bundle of abelian groups, then $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$ is non-commutative. To see this, assume first that there exists $e\in \mathcal{E}$ with $r(e)\neq s(e)$. Let $h\in C_0(G^{(0)})$ with $h(r(e))=1$ and $h(s(e))=0$ and $f\in C_c(G;\mathcal{E})$ with $f(e)\neq 0$ and $\pi(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f))$ a bisection (Lemma~\ref{lem:Urysohn}). Then
  \[
  (h\ast f)(e)  
    =h(r(e))f(e)=
  f(e)
  \neq
  0
  =f(e)h(s(e))=
    (f\ast h)(e),
  \]
  so $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$ is not commutative.
  
  Next, assume $e_{1},e_{2}\in \mathcal{E}(u)$ for some $u\in G^{(0)}$ are such that $e_{1}e_{2}\neq e_{2}e_{1}$. Take elements $f_{i}\in C_c(G;\mathcal{E})$ with $\pi(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f_{i}))$ a bisection and $f_{i}(e_{i}) \neq 0$, so that
  \[
    (f_{1}\ast f_{2})(e_{1}e_{2}) = f_{1}(e_{1})f_{2}(e_{2}) \neq 0.
  \]
  On the other hand, 
  \[
    (f_{2}\ast f_{1})(e_{1}e_{2}) = 
    \sum_{\{\,\pi(e)\in G:r(e)=u\,\}} f_{2}(e)f_{1}(e^{-1} e_{1}e_{2}).
  \]
  By assumption, $\pi(e_{2})$ is the unique element of $G_u\cap \pi(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f_{2}))$, so that
  \[
      (f_{2}\ast f_{1})(e_{1}e_{2})
      =
      f_{2}(e_{2})f_{1}(e_{2}^{-1} e_{1}e_{2}).
  \]
  If $\pi(e_{2}^{-1} e_{1}e_{2})\neq \pi(e_{1})$, then $f(e_{2}^{-1} e_{1}e_{2})=0$ and thus
  \[
    (f_{2}\ast f_{1})(e_{1}e_{2})
    =
    0
    \neq
    (f_{1}\ast f_{2})(e_{1}e_{2}).
  \]
  If $\pi(e_{2}^{-1} e_{1}e_{2})= \pi(e_{1})$, then by the assumption that $e_{1}e_{2}\neq e_{2}e_{1}$,  there exists $z\in\mathbf{T} \setminus\{\,1\,\}$ such that $e_{2}^{-1} e_{1}e_{2}=z\cdot e_{1}$, so that
  \[
    (f_{2}\ast f_{1})(e_{1}e_{2})
    =
    f_{2}(e_{2})f_{1}(z\cdot e_{1})
    =
    z f_{1}(e_{1}) f_{2}(e_{2})
    \neq
    f_{1}(e_{1}) f_{2}(e_{2})
    =
    (f_{1}\ast f_{2})(e_{1}e_{2}).
  \]
    In both cases, we conclude $f_{1}\ast f_{2}\neq f_{2}\ast f_{1}$.

label: lem-bisec-span
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-bisec-span} The space $C_{c}(G;\mathcal{E})$ is spanned by
  functions whose support is the preimage under $\pi$ of a bisection
  of~$G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f\in C_{c}(G; \mathcal{E})$.  Since $G$ is {\'e}tale, it has a basis of
  open bisections for its topology
  \cite{Renault:gpd-approach}*{Proposition~I.2.8}.  Since $\operatorname{supp}(f)$
  is compact, $\pi(\operatorname{supp}(f))$ can be covered with finitely many
  precompact open bisections $U_{1},\dots, U_{n}$.  Let
  $\{\phi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ be a partition of unity in
  $C_{c}^{+}(G)$ subordinate as in \cite{wil:crossed}*{Lemma~1.43} for
  $\{U_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$.  Then
  $f_{i}=(\phi_{i}\circ\pi)\cdot f\in C_{c}(G;\mathcal{E})$ has
  $\operatorname{supp} f_{i} \subset \pi^{-1}(U_{i})$ and satisfies
  $f=\sum_{i} f_{i}$.

label: prop-bfpr
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-bfpr}Let
  $\mathcal{E}$ be a twist over an {\'e}tale\ grou\-poid $G$.  Then there is a
  norm-decreasing linear map
  $j_{G}\colon \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})\to C_{0}(G;\mathcal{E})$ such that
  $j_{G}(f)(e)=f(e)$ if $f\in C_{c}(G;\mathcal{E})$.  Furthermore, for all
  $a,b\in \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$ we have
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:7}
    j_{G}(a^{*})(e)=\overline{j_{G}(a)(e^{-1} )} \quad\text{and} \quad
    j_{G}(ab)(e') =\sum_{\{\,\pi(e)\in G:r(e)=r(e')\,\}} j_{G}(a)(e)
    j_{G}(b)(e^{-1} e') .
  \end{equation}

label: def-cartan
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def-cartan}A
  \ensuremath{C^{*}}-subalgebra $B$ of a \ensuremath{C^{*}}-algebra $A$ is called \emph{Cartan} if
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $B$ is maximal abelian,
  \item $B$ is regular, meaning that the set
    \[N(B)=\{\,n\in A:
     \text{$nBn^{*}\subset B$ and $n^{*}Bn\subset B$}
        \,\}\] of \emph{normalizers} of $B$ generates
    $A$ as a \ensuremath{C^{*}}-algebra, and
  \item there is a faithful conditional expectation
    $\Phi\colon A\to B$.
  \end{enumerate}

label: lem:int is sbgpd
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:int is sbgpd}
    Suppose $G$ is a locally compact, Hausdorff\  groupoid with open range map, and let $\mathcal{E}$ be a twist over $G$ as in \eqref{eq:50}.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
    \item\label{it:int(H)} If $H$ is a subgroupoid of $G$, then so is $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left(H\right)$, and $\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\pi^{-1}(H)\right)=\mathcal{E}_{\operatorname{int}_{G}\left(H\right)}$.
    \item\label{item:saturation still abelian} If $\mathcal{F}$ is a
      subgroupoid of $\mathcal{E}$, then so is $\pi^{-1} (\pi(\mathcal{F}))$. If
      $\mathcal{F}$ is abelian, then so is $\pi^{-1} (\pi(\mathcal{F}))$.
    \item\label{item:int of IsoE vs int of IsoG}
      $\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left({\mathcal{E}'}\right)=
      \mathcal{E}_{\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)}
      $ and
      $\pi(\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left({\mathcal{E}'}\right))=\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$. In particular,
      $\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left({\mathcal{E}'}\right)$ is a subgroupoid of~$\mathcal{E}$.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

parts.label: item:int of IsoE vs int of IsoG

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{it:int(H)}
As the inversion map of  $G$ is a homeomorphism, it restricts to a map on $H^\circ \coloneq \operatorname{int}_{G}\left(H\right)$.
 Since the range map of $G$ is open,
  its multiplication map is open by \cite{Sims:gpds}*{Lemma 8.4.11}, so it restricts to a multiplication map on $H^\circ$, proving that $H^\circ$ is a subgroupoid of~$G$.
  Since $\pi$ is continuous, we have
  \[
    \mathcal{E}_{H^\circ}
    =
    \pi^{-1} (H^\circ)
    \subset
    \operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\pi^{-1}(H)\right)
    .
  \]
  For the other inclusion, note that $\pi(\pi^{-1}(H))=H$ by surjectivity of $\pi$, so since $\pi$ is an open map, we have
  \[
    \pi(\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\pi^{-1}(H)\right)) \subset H^\circ,
  \]
  which implies
  \[
    \operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\pi^{-1}(H)\right)
    =:
    V
    \subset 
    \pi^{-1}(\pi(V)) \subset \pi^{-1} (H^\circ)
    =
    \mathcal{E}_{H^\circ},
  \]
  as claimed.


  
    \ref{item:saturation still abelian} Because $\pi$ is a groupoid
    homomorphism, $\pi(\mathcal{F})$ is a subgroupoid of~$G$. Therefore,
    $\pi^{-1} (\pi(\mathcal{F}))$ is a subgroupoid of $\mathcal{E}$ by
    \cite{AMP:IsoThmsGpds}*{Proposition 9}. Now assume that $\mathcal{F}$ is
    abelian. For any $e \in \pi^{-1} (\pi(\mathcal{F}))$, there exists
    $e' \in \mathcal{F}$ such that $\pi(e) = \pi(e')$.  Since $\mathcal{F}$ is
    abelian, we have that $r(e)=r(e')$ coincides with $s(e)=s(e')$,
    proving that $\pi^{-1} (\pi(\mathcal{F})) \subset {\mathcal{E}'}$. To see that
    $\pi^{-1} (\pi(\mathcal{F}))$ is abelian, fix
    $e_1,e_2 \in \pi^{-1} (\pi(\mathcal{F}))$.  Then there exists
    $e_1',e_2' \in \mathcal{F}$ and $z_1,z_2 \in \mathbf{T}$ such that
    $e_1 = z_1\cdot e_1'$ and $e_2 = z_2\cdot e_2'$.  Since $\mathcal{E}$ is a
    central extension
    \begin{align*}
      e_1e_2 &= (z_1 \cdot e_1')(  z_2\cdot e_2') = (z_1z_2)\cdot (e_1' e_2')
      \\
      \intertext{which, since $\mathcal{F}$ is abelian, is}
             &= (z_2z_1)\cdot (e_2' e_1') \\
             &= (z_2 \cdot e_2')( z_1 \cdot e_1') = e_2 e_1,
    \end{align*}
    so $\pi^{-1} (\pi(\mathcal{F}))$ is abelian.
    
    \ref{item:int of IsoE vs int of IsoG} 
    The claim that $\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left({\mathcal{E}'}\right)=\mathcal{E}_{\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)}$ follows from Part~\ref{it:int(H)} applied to $H={G'}$ and from the fact that ${\mathcal{E}'}=\pi^{-1}({G'})$ since $\pi$ preserves ranges and sources.
    The
    equality $\pi(\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left({\mathcal{E}'}\right))=\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ now follows
    from surjectivity of $\pi$. 
    By Part~\ref{it:int(H)}, $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ is a subgroupoid of~$G$
    and so
    \( \operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left({\mathcal{E}'}\right)=\pi^{-1}(\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)) \) is a
    subgroupoid of $\mathcal{E}$, again by \cite{AMP:IsoThmsGpds}*{Proposition
    9}.

label: def:Ad_S,Omega
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:Ad_S,Omega}
    Assume $\mathcal{E}$ is a twist as in \eqref{eq:50} over a locally compact, Hausdorff\ groupoid $G$. Assume $S$ is an open subgroupoid of $G$. For $u\in G^{(0)}$ and $e\in \mathcal{E}(u)$, write
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)
        \coloneq
        \{\,
            \tau^{-1} e \tau : \tau\in \mathcal{E}_{S}(u)
        \,\},
    \end{equation}
    with the understanding that
    $\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)=\emptyset$ if $u\notin S^{(0)}$.
    Note that the set $\pi(\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e))$ does not depend on $e$ but only on $\pi(e)$, so we may let
    \[
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))\coloneq \pi(\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e))
        .
    \]
    Let $\overline{\mathbf{N}}=\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}\cup\{\,\infty\,\}$ denote the extended natural numbers, and define $\Omega_{S}\colon {\mathcal{E}'}\to\overline{\mathbf{N}}$ for $e\in {\mathcal{E}'}$ by
  \[
    \Omega_{S}(e) =
    \begin{cases}
        \left|\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)\right|,&\text{ if }  \left| \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)\right| = \left|\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))\right|<\infty,        
        \\
        \infty&\text{ otherwise.}
    \end{cases}
  \]
  In other words, $\Omega_S(e)$ checks whether or not $\pi$ is injective on the set $\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)$, and whether $\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))$ is finite.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In the case where $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{E}_c$ is given by a $2$-cocycle $c$, an equality of the form $(t,w)^{-1} (g,z) (t,w)=(g,z)$ in $\mathcal{E}_{c}$ implies not only that $t^{-1} gt=g$ but also that $c(g,t)=c(t,g)$. It is easy to see in examples
that the condition $c(g,t)=c(t,g)$ is \emph{not} implied by $t^{-1} g t=g$.
In other words, the equality $\tau^{-1} e\tau = e$ in 
any twist
$\mathcal{E}$ is a stronger condition than $\pi(\tau)^{-1} \pi(e) \pi(\tau) = \pi(e)$ in $G$, and we can 
in general
only deduce $|\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)|\geq|\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))|$.
In Example~\ref{ex:rotation}, the reader can find an example in which this inequality is strict, since there, the entire groupoid $G$ is abelian, but the twist is not.

\label{rmk:intG subgpd}
  It follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:int is sbgpd}\ref{it:int(H)}
  that $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ is a subgroupoid of~$G$. Note further that, since $\pi$ is a groupoid homomorphism, $\mathcal{E}_{S}$ is
  subgroupoid of~$\mathcal{E}$. 
  Therefore it is reasonable to
  talk about $S$ being a maximal open subgroupoid \emph{of the interior of  ${G'}$} for
  which $\mathcal{E}_{S}$ is abelian, as we have done in
  Item~\ref{it:thm:May17:S:Omega+max}.

title: Remark
body_md:
The `gate keeper' $\Omega_{S}$ is assessing whether or not ${\mathcal{E}'}$ has points $e$ that stand in the way of $B\coloneq i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))$ being maximal abelian in $A\coloneq\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r} (G;\mathcal{E})$ (see Proposition~\ref{prop:max_new}).
    
    
    By comparing the statements in~\ref{it:thm:May17:S:Omega} and \ref{it:thm:May17:S:Omega+max} of Theorem~\ref{thm:May17}, one can see that 
    Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:Int Omega=1} 
    ensures that $B$ is maximal among the abelian subalgebras of $A$ that arise from open subgroupoids
    (see Corollary~\ref{cor:S max in terms of Omega}) 
     
    , hence the name of the condition.
    On the other hand, in Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:icc}, the map $\Omega_{S}$ discerns whether there are points $e\in{\mathcal{E}'}$ for which
    \[
    1 < |\{\sigma^{-1} e\sigma:\sigma \in \mathcal{E}_{S}\}|= |\{s^{-1} \pi(e)s:s \in S\}|<\infty;
    \]
    i.e., points $e$ that do not have {\em relative infinite conjugacy class} (relative with respect to the subgroupoid $S$). The
    proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:max_new}  
    shows why an open set of such points stands
     in the way of $B$ being maximal
     (the key is the technical result in Lemma~\ref{lem:fancy lemma}).
     Let us briefly explain here why those points for which $\Omega_S(e)$ takes the value $\infty$, do not `pose a threat' to the maximality of $B$.
   
    There are two scenarios in which $\Omega_S(e)=\infty$. In the first, $\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)$  has cardinality larger than that of $\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi (e ))$, so
    there exists $\sigma\in\mathcal{E}_{S}$ such that $\sigma^{-1} e\sigma \neq e$ but $\pi(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma)=\pi(e)$, i.e., $\sigma^{-1} e\sigma = z\cdot e$ for some $z\in \mathbf{T}\setminus\{1\}$. With this condition, any $h\in 
    C_c
    (G;\mathcal{E})$ with $e\in \operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(h)$ satisfies
    \[
    0
    \neq
    zh(e) = h(z\cdot e) =  h(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma).
    \]
    As $z\neq 1$, this proves $h(e)\neq h(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma)$. We will see in Lemma~\ref{lem:conjugation equality} that $h$ therefore does not commute with 
    $B$.
    In other words, there is no element of $A$ that both commutes with $B$ and does not vanish at $e$, and
     so the existence of $e$
    cannot be the cause of $B$ not being maximal abelian in $A$.

    
    The second scenario in which $\Omega_S(e)$ takes on the value $\infty$, is when $\operatorname{Ad}_S(\pi(e))$ (and hence $\operatorname{Ad}_S(e)$) is infinite. If $h\in
    C_c
    (G;\mathcal{E})$ commutes with $
    B
    $, then the reverse implication of Lemma~\ref{lem:conjugation equality} states that $h(e)=h(e')$ for every $e'\in \operatorname{Ad}_S(e)$. But since the isotropy groups of $G$ are discrete and since  $\operatorname{Ad}_S(\pi(e))$ is infinite, this implies that $h(e)=0$. 
    So
    again, $e$ cannot be the cause of $B$ not being maximal abelian.

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $S$ and $G$ be as specified in Theorem~\ref{thm:May17}\ref{it:thm:May17:S:Omega+max}.
    According to \cite{ren:irms08}, the Cartan pair $i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})) \subset \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$  gives rise to a Weyl groupoid and Weyl twist, and one may wonder how it relates to the pair $S\subset G$.
    
    In the case that $\mathcal{E}$ is induced by a $2$-cocycle,  \cite{DGN:Weyl} identified the effective Weyl groupoid as a certain transformation groupoid and, assuming that the quotient map $G\to G/S$ allows a continuous section, the Weyl twist was identified as a certain $2$-cocycle. The recent pre-print \cite{BG:2023:Gamma-Cartan-pp} extends those $2$-cocycle results to the setting of $\Gamma$-Cartan pairs from subgroupoids of $\Gamma$-graded groupoids. 

    It is somewhat straight forward to prove that, in the setting of
    Theorem~\ref{thm:May17}\ref{it:thm:May17:S:Omega+max},
    the Weyl groupoid can likewise be identified as a transformation groupoid of a continuous action by the quotient groupoid $G/S$ on the Gelfand dual of $i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})) $. Moreover, this dual can be described in terms of $\mathcal{E}_{S}$,  along the same lines of what is done in \cite{DGN:Weyl}*{Section 3} 
    in the $2$-cocycle case.
    The Weyl twist, on the other hand, is more elusive. We deal with a detailed description of both the Weyl groupoid and the Weyl twist in a separate paper
     
    \cite{D:2025:DGNvsDWZ-inprep}; the interested reader can also find a related result in \cite{Renault:2023:Ext}*{Theorem 5.5}. In \cite{D:2025:DGNvsDWZ-inprep}, we also answer the question when a normal subgroupoid gives rise to a $\ensuremath{C^{*}}$-diagonal, i.e., a Cartan subalgebra with the unique extension property.

title: Proof
body_md:
If a subgroupoid $S$ is abelian, then it is contained in ${G'}$. If it is open, it is contained in $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$. If $G$ is effective, the latter equals $G^{(0)}$, meaning $S=r(S)$ is trivial. 
    
    Conversely, assume $G$ 
    is non-effective. Since $G$ is {\'e}tale, this means we can find a non-empty open bisection $V\subset  G\setminus G^{(0)}$ such that $V\subset  {G'}$. Since $V$ is a bisection, we have $V=\bigsqcup_{u\in r(V)} \{g_u\}$, where $V\cap G(u)=\{g_u\}$. Since the $g_u$'s do not interact with one another, the  subgroupoid 
     $\langle V\rangle$ of $G$ generated by $V$ is exactly the bundle $\bigsqcup_{u\in r(V)}\langle g_u\rangle$ of abelian groups generated by the individual $g_u$, so $\langle V\rangle$ is an abelian subgroupoid of ${G'}$. Since $V$ is open, $S\coloneq\operatorname{int}_{G}\left(\langle V\rangle\right)$ contains $V$.
  By
  Lemma~\ref{lem:int is sbgpd}\ref{it:int(H)},
  $S$ is an open subgroupoid of $G$; as $\langle V\rangle$ is abelian, so is $S$; and as $\emptyset \neq V\subset  S\cap (G\setminus G^{(0)})$, $S$ is non-trivial.

label: prop:CondExp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:CondExp}
  Suppose  
  the subgroupoid 
 $S$ is not only open but also closed
 in $G$.
 Define
  $\Phi_0\colon C_c(G;\mathcal{E}) \to C_c(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$ by
  $ \Phi_0(f) \coloneq f|_{{\mathcal{E}_{S}}}$. 
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
  \item\label{it:CondExp:Phi_0 extends} $\Phi_0$ extends to a linear map
    $ \Phi\colon \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E}) \to \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$.
  \item\label{it:CondExp:i circ Phi} The map $ i \circ\Phi$ is a conditional expectation from
    $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$ to $ i (\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))$.
  \item\label{it:CondExp:j-maps} We have
    $j_{S}(\Phi(a)) = j_G(a)|_{{\mathcal{E}_{S}}}$ for all
    $a \in \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$.
  \item\label{it:CondExp:faithful} If $S^{(0)}=G^{(0)}$, then $\Phi(a^*a)=0$ implies $a=0$, so
    $ i \circ\Phi$ is faithful.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: cf.\ *{Lemma 3.4

title: Proof
body_md:
Both~\ref{it:CondExp:Phi_0 extends} and~\ref{it:CondExp:i circ Phi} are contained in \cite{BEFPR:2021:Intermediate}*{Lemma 3.4}.
For completion, we add a proof here. We will follow the ideas of the proof of \cite{DGNRW:Cartan}*{Proposition 3.13}. 

\ref{it:CondExp:Phi_0 extends} Because $S$ is closed and $\pi$ is continuous,
  $\pi^{-1}(S) = \mathcal{E}_{S}$ is closed, so that $\Phi_{0}$ is well defined.
  For $u\in G^{(0)}$, let $H^{G}_{u}\coloneq \ell^2(G_{u};\mathcal{E}_{u})$ and
  $\theta^{G}_{u}\colon C_c(G;\mathcal{E}) \to B\left(H^{G}_{u}\right)$, the
  regular representations from~\eqref{eq:5} for $\mathcal{E}$; we analogously
  define $H^{S}_{u}\coloneq \ell^2(S_{u};(\mathcal{E}_{S})_{u})$ and
  $\theta^{S}_{u}$ for $u\in S^{(0)}$.  Let
  $P \in B\left(H^{G}_{u}\right)$ be the projection onto the subspace
  of elements that vanish outside of the (potentially empty) subset
  $\mathcal{E}_{S}\cap \mathcal{E}_{u}$. Note that there is a canonical unitary
  $F\colon H^{S}_{u} \to PH^{G}_{u}$. For $f\in C_c(G;\mathcal{E})$ and
  $\xi\in H^{S}_{u}$, we claim that
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:theta-G and theta-S}
    P \theta^{G}_{u}(f) (F(\xi)) = F\left(
      \theta^{S}_{u}(f|_{{\mathcal{E}_{S}}})(\xi)\right). 
  \end{equation}
  By construction, both sides are elements of $PH^{G}_{u}$, and so
  they vanish outside of $\mathcal{E}_{S}$. At $e\in \mathcal{E}_{S}$, we have
  \begin{align*} [P \theta^{G}_{u}(f) (F(\xi))](e) &=
    \sum_{\{\,\pi(e_{1})\in G: r(e)=r(e_{1})\,\}} f(ee_{1}^{-1})\,
    F(\xi)(e_{1})
    \\
       &=
         \sum_{\{\,\pi(e_{1})\in
         S:
         r(e)=r(e_{1})\,\}}
         f(ee_{1}^{-1})\,
         \xi(e_{1})
    \\
       &\overset{(\dagger)}{=}
         \sum_{\{\,\pi(e_{1})\in
         G:
         r(e)=r(e_{1})\,\}}
         f|_{{\mathcal{E}_{S}}}(ee_{1}^{-1})\,
         \xi(e_{1})
    \\
       &= [F\left(
         \theta^{S}_{u}(f|_{{\mathcal{E}_{S}}})(\xi)\right)](e). 
  \end{align*}
  Here, $(\dagger)$ follows from the fact that $\pi(e_{1})\in S$ if
  and only if $ee_{1}^{-1}\in \mathcal{E}_{S}$, since $e\in \mathcal{E}_{S}$ and since
  $\mathcal{E}_{S}$ is a subgroupoid. 
  This proves~\eqref{eq:theta-G and theta-S}. It 
  follows that
\begin{align*}
    \|\theta^{S}_{u} (f|_{{\mathcal{E}_{S}}})\|
    &=
    \sup\left\{\|F\left(
      \theta^{S}_{u}(f|_{{\mathcal{E}_{S}}})(\xi)\right)\| : \xi\in H^{S}_{u},
      \|\xi\|=1\right\}
      &&
      \text{since $F$ is a unitary}
    \\
    &\leq
    \sup\left\{\|\theta^{G}_{u}(f) (F(\xi))\| : \xi\in H^{S}_{u},
      \|\xi\|=1\right\}
      &&
      \text{by \eqref{eq:theta-G and theta-S}}
      \\
    &\leq
    \sup\left\{\|\theta^{G}_{u}(f) (\eta)\| : \eta\in H^{G}_{u},
      \|\eta\|=1\right\} 
    =
    \|\theta^{G}_{u}(f)\|.
\end{align*}
Since $u\in S^{(0)}\subset  G^{(0)}$ was arbitrary, this shows that
$\|\Phi_{0}(f)\|_{r}\leq \|f\|_{r}$. 
  
Thus, $\|\Phi_0\| \leq 1$, so that $\Phi_0$ extends to a continuous
linear map $\Phi\colon \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E}) \to
\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$. 

    

\ref{it:CondExp:i circ Phi}
Clearly, $\Phi_0\circ i $ is the identity on $C_c(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$, so
that $ i \circ \Phi\circ i = i $. It follows that
$\mathmbox{i\circ\Phi}                                                      
\colon \ensuremath{C^{*}}_r(G;\mathcal{E})\to\ensuremath{C^{*}}_r(G;\mathcal{E})$ maps onto and
fixes the subalgebra $ i (\ensuremath{C^{*}}_r(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))$ of
$\ensuremath{C^{*}}_r(G;\mathcal{E})$. Since $ i \circ\Phi$ is furthermore contractive
and linear, it follows from \cite{BrOz:FinDimApp}*{Theorem 1.5.10}
that it is a conditional expectation.
       
\ref{it:CondExp:j-maps}
To see that $j_{S}(\Phi(a)) = j_G(a)|_{{\mathcal{E}_{S}}}$ for all
$a \in \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$, note that the claim is trivial for
$a\in C_c(G;\mathcal{E})$: in this case, $\Phi(a)=a|_{{\mathcal{E}_{S}}}$, and the
maps $j_{G}$ and $j_{S}$ are just the inclusions of $C_c(G;\mathcal{E})$
and $C_c(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$ into $C_0(G;\mathcal{E})$ resp.\
$C_0(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$. Continuity of all maps involved implies the
claim
for arbitrary $a$.


\ref{it:CondExp:faithful}
Assume $S^{(0)}=G^{(0)}$. To see that $\Phi$ is faithful, recall that
\cite{ren:irms08}*{Proposition 4.3} says that the map
$C_c(G;\mathcal{E})\to C_0 (G^{(0)}), f\mapsto f|_{{G^{(0)}}}$, extends to a faithful
conditional expectation $P_{G}\colon \ensuremath{C^{*}}_r(G;\mathcal{E})\to C_0 (G^{(0)})$.
The  diagram
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}
        \ensuremath{C^{*}}_r(G;\mathcal{E}) \ar[rr, "P_{G}"] \ar[rd, "\Phi"'] && C_0 (G^{(0)})
        \\
        & \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}) \ar[ru, "P_{S}"'] &
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    commutes since it commutes on the dense subspace $C_{c}
    (G;\mathcal{E})$.
    If $\Phi(a^*a)=0$, then commutativity implies $P_{G}(a^*a)=0$, so
    $a=0$ since $P_{G}$ is faithful.

body_md:
\label{rmk:G amenable}
  If $G$ is amenable, then the assumption in Proposition~\ref{prop:support in S} that $S$ be closed is not needed to conclude equality of the sets; see
   
  \cite{BEFPR:2024:Corrigendum}.
     Our proof, however, heavily
  relies on the conditional expectation
  constructed in Proposition~\ref{prop:CondExp} which, by \cite{BEFPR:2021:Intermediate}*{Lemma 3.4},
  exists if and only if $S$ is closed.

title: Proof
body_md:
First, note that
  $B\coloneq\{\,b \in \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E}): \operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(j_{G}(b)) \subset 
  \mathcal{E}_{S}\,\}$ is closed: if $\{b_n\}$ is a sequence in $B$
  converging to $b \in \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$, and if
  $e \in
  \mathcal{E}\setminus\mathcal{E}_{S}$, 
  then continuity of $j_{G}$ implies that
  $0=j_G(b_n)(e)\to j_G(b)(e)$, so $j_G(b)(e) = 0$.

  For $f \in C_c(S; \mathcal{E}_{S})$,
  $\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(j_{G}(i(f))) = \operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f)$ is a subset of $\mathcal{E}_{S}$, so
  $i(C_c(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})) \subset  B$. Since $B$ is closed, since
  $i$ is continuous, and since $C_c(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$ is dense in
  $ \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$, we conclude
  $i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})) \subset  B$.

  Now fix $b \in B$
  and assume that $S$ is clopen, so that
  we can consider the (not
  necessarily faithful) map
  $ \Phi\colon \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E}) \to \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$ from
  Proposition~\ref{prop:CondExp}. If
  $i'\colon C_0(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})\to C_0(G;\mathcal{E})$ denotes the
  inclusion as in Lemma~\ref{lem:j-map commutes},
  then 
  we have
\begin{align*}
   j_G(b)
   &=
   i'(j_G(b)|_{{\mathcal{E}_{S}}})
   &&\text{since $\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(j_G(b))\subset  \mathcal{E}_{S}$}
   \\
   &= i'(j_{S}(\Phi(b)))
   &&\text{by Proposition~\ref{prop:CondExp}\ref{it:CondExp:j-maps}} 
   \\ 
   &= j_G(i(\Phi(b)))
   &&\text{by Lemma~\ref{lem:j-map commutes}}.
\end{align*}
Since $j_G$ is injective, we conclude $b = i(\Phi(b))\in
i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))$.

label: lem:S max implies
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:S max implies}
     Assume that $S$ is
      maximal among open subgroupoids of $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ for which
      $\mathcal{E}_{S}$ is abelian. 
      If $X\subset {G'}$ is open and for each $e\in \pi^{-1}(X)$ and $\sigma\in \mathcal{E}_{S}(r(e))$, we have $e\sigma=\sigma e$, then $X\subset S$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We adapt the proof of \cite{BG:2023:Gamma-Cartan-pp}*{Proposition 3.4} to the case of general twists. Fix $e\in \pi^{-1}(X)$. Since $G$ is {\'e}tale\ and $X$ is open, there exists an open bisection $Y\subset X$ around $\pi(e)$. Let $\mathcal{F}\coloneq \langle \mathcal{E}_{S}, \pi^{-1}(Y)\rangle$ be the subgroupoid of ${\mathcal{E}'}$ generated by $\mathcal{E}_{S}$ and $\pi^{-1}(Y)$. By assumption on $X$ and since $Y\subset X$, every element of $\pi^{-1}(Y)$ commutes with every element of $\mathcal{E}_{S}$. Moreover, if $\tau_{1},\tau_{2}\in \pi^{-1}(Y)$ are composable, then since $Y$ is a bisection contained in ${G'}$, there exists $z\in\mathbf{T} $ such that $\tau_{1}=z\cdot \tau_{2}$; since the $\mathbf{T}$-action is central, this means that $\tau_{1}$ and $\tau_{2}$ commute. Since $\mathcal{E}_{S}$ is abelian by assumption, it follows that $\mathcal{F}$ is an abelian subgroupoid of $\mathcal{E}$. 

    Since $(\pi(e_{1}),\pi(e_{2}))\in G^{(2)} $ implies that
    $(e_{1},e_{2})\in \mathcal{E}^{(2)} $, it follows from \cite{AMP:IsoThmsGpds}*{Proposition
    10} that 
    $\pi(\mathcal{F})$ is a
    subgroupoid of ${G'}$, and it follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:int is sbgpd}\ref{item:saturation still
      abelian} that $\pi^{-1} (\pi(\mathcal{F}))$  is abelian.    
    By Lemma~\ref{lem:int is sbgpd}\ref{it:int(H)}, $T\coloneq \operatorname{int}_{G}\left(\pi(\mathcal{F})\right)$ is an open subgroupoid of $G$ and
    \[
        \operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\pi^{-1}(\pi(\mathcal{F}))\right) 
        \overset{\text{L.~\ref{lem:int is sbgpd}}}{=} \mathcal{E}_{T}
        \subset
        \pi^{-1} (\pi(\mathcal{F})),
    \]
    which implies that the twist $\mathcal{E}_{T}$ is abelian.

    By definition of $\mathcal{F}$, it contains $\mathcal{E}_{S}$ and $\pi^{-1}(Y)$. Since $S$ and $Y$ are open, we conclude $\mathcal{E}_{S},\pi^{-1}(Y)\subset \operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\mathcal{F}\right)$, so $S$ and $Y$ are subsets of $\pi(\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\mathcal{F}\right))$. Since $\pi$ is open, this set is contained in $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left(\pi(\mathcal{F})\right)=T$, so $S,Y\subset T$.  Since $T$ is an open subgroupoid of ${G'}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{T}$ is abelian, maximality of~$S$
    implies that $S=T$. Thus $\pi(e)\in Y\subset T=S$. Since $\pi(e)\in X$ was arbitrary, this proves that $X\subset S$.

body_md:
\label{cor:S max in terms of Omega}
    The following are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
      \item\label{item:cor:S max implied by} 
      $S$ satisfies Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:Int Omega=1}, i.e., 
      $G^{(0)}\subset S$ and
      $\mathcal{E}_{S}=\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\Omega_{S}^{-1}(\{\,1\,\})\right)$.
      \item\label{item:cor:S max implies} $S$ is

labels: cor:S max in terms of Omega

title: Proof
body_md:
Note first that, if $T$ is a subgroupoid of $G$ for which $\mathcal{E}_{T}$ is abelian, then $\mathcal{E}_{T}$ is contained in ${\mathcal{E}'}$ and any $\tau\in\mathcal{E}_{T}$ satisfies
    \[
        \operatorname{Ad}_{T}(\tau)
        =
        \{\,
            \sigma^{-1} \tau  \sigma : \sigma\in \mathcal{E}_{T}
        \,\}
        =
        \{\,\tau\,\}.
    \]
    If $T$ is open, then $\mathcal{E}_{T}$ is contained in $\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left({\mathcal{E}'}\right)$, so that $\mathcal{E}_{T}\subset \operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\Omega_{T}^{-1}(\{\,1\,\})\right)$. 

    

    \ref{item:cor:S max implied by}$\implies$\ref{item:cor:S max implies}: Let $T$ be
    open and
    as above. If $S\subset T$, then $T^{(0)}=G^{(0)}$ and
    $\mathcal{E}_{S}\subset \mathcal{E}_{T}$, so that
    \begin{align*}
        \Omega_{T}^{-1} (\{\,1\,\})
        &=
        \bigsqcup_{u\in G^{(0)}}
        \{\,
            e\in \mathcal{E}(u):\forall\tau\in \mathcal{E}_{T}(u), e\tau=\tau e
        \,\}
        \\        
        &\subset
        \bigsqcup_{u\in G^{(0)}}
        \{\,
            e\in \mathcal{E}(u):\forall\sigma\in \mathcal{E}_{S}(u), e\sigma=\sigma e
        \,\}
        =\Omega_{S}^{-1} (\{\,1\,\}).
    \end{align*}
    The previous paragraph
    shows
    $(\dagger)$ in the following:
    \[
        \mathcal{E}_{S}\subset \mathcal{E}_{T} 
        \overset{(\dagger)}{\subset} \operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\Omega_{T}^{-1}\{\,1\,\}\right)
        \subset \operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\Omega_{S}^{-1}(\{\,1\,\})\right)
        \overset{\ref{item:cor:S max implied by}}{=}
        \mathcal{E}_{S},
    \]
    so  $\mathcal{E}_{S}=\mathcal{E}_{T}$ and thus $S=T$.
    
    

    \ref{item:cor:S max implies}$\implies$\ref{item:cor:S max implied by}:    
    Since $G$ is {\'e}tale, $G^{(0)}$ is clopen, and so $T\coloneq S\cup G^{(0)}$
  is a clopen subgroupoid of $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ for which the
  restricted twist $\mathcal{E}_{T}$ is abelian. By maximality of~$S$, we conclude $S^{(0)}=G^{(0)}$. 
    If 
    $e_0\in \operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\Omega_{S}^{-1}(\{\,1\,\})\right)$, then 
    we can find an open neighborhood $V$ of $e_0$ such that $V\subset \Omega_{S}^{-1}(\{\,1\,\})$. In particular, $V\subset {\mathcal{E}'}$ and for each $e\in V$ and composable $\sigma\in \mathcal{E}_{S}$, we have  $\sigma^{-1} e\sigma =e$. Now consider $X\coloneq \pi(V)$. If $e'\in \pi^{-1}(X)$, then there exists $e\in V$ and $z\in\mathbf{T} $ such that $e'
    =z\cdot e$. In particular,
    \[
    \sigma^{-1} e'\sigma =
    \sigma^{-1} (z\cdot e)\sigma
    =
    z\cdot (\sigma^{-1} e\sigma)
    =
    z\cdot e = e'.
    \]
    This shows that every element $e'$ of $\pi^{-1}(X)$ likewise commutes with all composable elements of $\mathcal{E}_{S}$.
    By Lemma~\ref{lem:S max implies},
    our assumption in \ref{item:cor:S max implies} implies that
    $X\subset S$, so $\pi^{-1}(X)\subset \mathcal{E}_{S}$.
    Since $e\in V\subset  \pi^{-1}(X)$ was an arbitrary point of $\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\Omega_{S}^{-1}(\{\,1\,\})\right)$, this
    proves that $\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\Omega_{S}^{-1}(\{\,1\,\})\right)\subset \mathcal{E}_{S}$. Since the reverse containment holds by the first paragraph, that concludes the proof.

label: lem:conjugation equality
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:conjugation equality}
  Suppose 
  $S\subset {G'}$ and let $h \in C_0(G;\mathcal{E})$ 
   
  with $\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(h)\subset {\mathcal{E}'}$.
    
  The following are equivalent.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
      \item\label{it:conj equ:commutes} For all $f \in C_c(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$, 
      we have $h*i(f) = i(f)* h$.
      \item\label{it:conj equ:constant on conjugates}  For all
        $u \in S^{(0)} $, $e \in \mathcal{E}(u) $, and $\sigma \in \mathcal{E}_{S}(u)$, we have $h(e) = h(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma)$.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: eq:h*i(f)
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $u \in S^{(0)} $, $e \in \mathcal{E}(u) $, and $\sigma \in \mathcal{E}_{S}(u)$.
  If
  $f \in C_c(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$, then
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:h*i(f)}
      [h * i(f)](e\sigma) = \sum_{\{\,\pi(e_{1})\in G:r(e_{1})= u \,\}}
    h(e_{1})i(f)( e_{1}^{-1} e\sigma).
  \end{equation}
    If $f\in C_{c}(G;\mathcal{E})$ is such that $f(\sigma)\neq 0$ and  $\pi(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f))$ is a bisection of
  $G$, then at most one summand in~\eqref{eq:h*i(f)} survives, namely
  that for $\pi(e_{1})$ with $\pi(e_{1}^{-1} e\sigma)=\pi(\sigma)$ so
  that
  \[ [h *i(f)](e\sigma) = h(e) f(\sigma).
  \]
  Similarly, in the sum
  \[ [i(f) *h](e\sigma) = \sum_{\{\,\pi(e_{1}) \in G: r(e_{1})=r(e)\,\}}
    i(f) (e_{1})\ h( e_{1}^{-1} e\sigma),
  \]
  only the summand for $\pi(e_{1})=\pi(\sigma)$ survives, which yields
  \[ [i (f) * h](e\sigma) = f(\sigma) h(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma).
  \]
    
  \ref{it:conj equ:commutes}$\implies$\ref{it:conj equ:constant on conjugates}:
  Fix $u,e,\sigma$ as above.
  Since $S$ is open and $G$ is {\'e}tale, $S$ is likewise {\'e}tale, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:Urysohn}, there exists an element $f$ 
  of $C_{c}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$ such that $f(\sigma)\neq 0$ and $\pi(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f))$ is a bisection.
  With the previous computation, we conclude that
    \[ h(e) f(\sigma)= [h*i(f)](e\sigma)\overset{\ref{it:conj equ:commutes}}{=} [i(f)*h](e\sigma)= f(\sigma) h(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma).\] 
    Since  $f(\sigma)\neq 0$, we deduce $h(e) = h(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma)$.

  

    \ref{it:conj equ:constant on conjugates}$\implies$\ref{it:conj equ:commutes}: 
    For any $f\in C_c(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$ with $\pi(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f))$ a bisection,
     
    first note that $h*i(f)$ and $i(f)*h$ both vanish on $\mathcal{E}\setminus{\mathcal{E}'}$, since we assume $h$ and $f$ to be supported in the isotropy, and they also both vanish on $\mathcal{E}(u)$ for $u\notin s(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f))$. So suppose $u\in s(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f))$; let $\sigma\in \operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(f)\cap \mathcal{E}_{S}(u)$. For $e\in \mathcal{E}(u)$,
     
     
    we have by the previous computation that
    \[
    [h*i(f)](e\sigma)=h(e) f(\sigma)\overset{\ref{it:conj equ:constant on conjugates}}{=}  f(\sigma) h(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma) = [i(f)*h](e\sigma)
    .\]
     
    Since any element $e'$ of $\mathcal{E}(u)$ can be written as $e'=(e'\sigma^{-1})\sigma$, the above proves that the $h*i(f)$ and $i(f)*h$ coincide on all of $\mathcal{E}(u)$.
    Since such $f$ span $C_c(S;\mathcal{E}_{S})$ by Lemma~\ref{lem-bisec-span}, we conclude 
    \ref{it:conj equ:commutes}.

   Assume that $S\subset {G'}$
   is abelian and
   fails to satisfy Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:icc}, i.e.,
   \[
   \operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\Omega_{S}^{-1} (\mathbf{Z}_{>1})\right)\neq \emptyset.
   \]
    Then there exist $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{>0}$, pairwise disjoint open bisections $V_{0},\ldots,V_{n} \subset {G'}\setminus S$ and  $\mathbf{T}$-equivariant homeomorphisms \[
        \Psi_{i}\colon \pi^{-1} (V_i) \to\pi^{-1} (V_0)
    \] 
   such that: 
       If  $e\in\pi^{-1}(V_{i})$ for some $i\in\{\,0,\ldots, n\,\}$ is composable with $\sigma \in \mathcal{E}_{S}$, then there exists a unique $j\in\{\,0,\ldots, n\,\}$ such that $\sigma^{-1} e\sigma\in\pi^{-1}(V_{j})$, and we have $\Psi_{i}(e)=\Psi_{j}(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the notation $\operatorname{Ad}_S$ and $\Omega_{S}$ from Definition~\ref{def:Ad_S,Omega}. 
     
    We start by assuming that $S\subset{G'}$ is abelian and that $X\subset {\mathcal{E}'}$ is a non-empty open set with $X\cap \mathcal{E}_{S}=\emptyset$ and such that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:new:property of X}
    N < \left|
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))
    \right|
        =
        \left| 
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)
        \right|
        < \infty
        \quad\text{for all }e\in X
    \end{equation}
    for some $N\in\{0,1,\ldots\}$.
    For any $z\in \mathbf{T}$ and $e\in{\mathcal{E}'}$, we have
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:Ad of ze}
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(z\cdot e) = \{\, z\cdot e' : e'\in \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)\,\},
    \end{equation}
    and thus in particular  $\Omega_{S}(z\cdot e)=\Omega_{S}(e)$. We can thus replace $X$ with $\pi^{-1}(\pi(X))$ without changing its property 
     
    at~\eqref{eq:new:property of X}.
    Note
    that~\eqref{eq:new:property of X}
    implies that $U\coloneq r(X)=s(X)$ is contained in~$S^{(0)}$, since $\Omega_{S}(e)=0$ for $e\in {\mathcal{E}'}$ with $s(e)\notin S^{(0)}$. 
     
    Since $X\cap \mathcal{E}_{S}=\emptyset$ by assumption,
    we have that $V_0\coloneq\pi(X)$ is contained in $  G\setminus S$.
     
     
     
    
    By shrinking $X$, we can assume that $V_0$ is a (necessarily open) bisection in $G$. 
  Since $V_0\subset G\setminus S$ and $V_0=\pi(X)\subset \pi(\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left({\mathcal{E}'}\right))$, it follows from 
  Lemma~\ref{lem:int is sbgpd}\ref{item:int of IsoE vs int of IsoG}
  that $V_0\subset \operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)\setminus S$.
   Let $g_0(\cdot)\colon U\to V_0$ be the  homeomorphism that sends $u\in U\subset S^{(0)}$
   to the unique element $g_0(u)$ in $V_0\cap G(u)\subset \pi(X)$.
    
    \begin{claim}\label{claim:lsc}
    The map $u\mapsto |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|$ is lower semi-continuous from $U$ to $\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$.
    \end{claim}

    \begin{proof}[Proof of Claim~\ref{claim:lsc}]
    Fix any $\overline{u}\in U
    \subset S^{(0)}
    $ and let $g_0\coloneq g_0(\overline{u})$. 
    It will suffice to find an open neighborhood $\tilde{U}\subset U$ of $\overline u$ such that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:lsc inequality}
    | \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|
    \geq 
    |
   \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(\overline{u}))|
    \end{equation} 
for all $u\in \tilde{U}$.
 
If $|\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0)|=N+1$, then since $g_0(u)\in \pi(X)$, Inequality~\eqref{eq:lsc inequality} follows automatically from the property at~\eqref{eq:new:property of X} of $X$, and we are done; therefore, we may assume that $n\coloneq |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0)|-1 
> N\geq 0
$,
 
so that 
    \[
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0)
        =
        \{\, g_0,g_1,\ldots,g_{n}\,\}
        \subset
        G(\overline{u})
    \]
    for pairwise distinct elements $g_{i}$.
     Since $G$ is Hausdorff,
    there is an open neighborhood $\tilde{U}$ of $\overline u$
    such that there exist 
    open
    bisections 
    $V_{1},\ldots, V_{n}$ for which $g_{i}\in V_{i}$ and $\tilde{U}=s(V_{i})$  for all $i\in\{\,1,\ldots, n\,\}$. We let $g_i(\cdot)$ denote the homeomorphisms from $\tilde{U}$ to $V_i$ sending $u$ to the unique element $g_i(u)\in V_i\cap G_u$; in particular, $g_{i}(\overline{u})=g_{i}\in G(\overline{u})$.

\begin{figure}[h]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[height=0.6\textheight]{DWZ_step1}
    \caption{We shrink the open bisections ( 
     
    drawn with solid lines
     
    in color on the left) around the $S$-conjugates $g_{0},\ldots, g_{n}$ to make them disjoint and homeomorphic ( 
     
    circular neighborhoods drawn with dashed lines
     
    ).}
    \label{fig:step1}
\end{figure}



    
   

    For any two distinct $i,j\in\{\,0,\ldots,n\,\}$, we have $g_{i}(\overline{u})=g_{i}\neq g_{j}=g_{j}(\overline{u})$, so by continuity 
    we can shrink $\tilde{U}$
    and
    assume that $g_{i}(u)\neq g_{j}(u)$ for all $u\in \tilde{U}$, meaning that the bisections $V_0\cap r^{-1} (\tilde{U}),V_{1},\ldots, V_{n}$ are pairwise disjoint; see Figure~\ref{fig:step1}.
  
    For each $u\in \tilde{U}$,
    we have $s(g_0(u))=u=r(g_0(u))$, so for each $i\in\{\,0,\ldots, n\,\}$, we may 
    consider the following pairwise disjoint subsets of $S(u)$: 
    \begin{align*}
    S_{i}(u)
    =
    \{\,
    t\in S(u): t^{-1} g_0(u)t=g_{i}(u)
    \,\},
    \end{align*}
    so that
    \begin{align}        
    \{\, t^{-1} g_{0}(u) t : t\in S_{i}(u)\,\}
    =
    \begin{cases}
    \emptyset,
    &
    \text{if }S_{i}(u)=\emptyset,
    \\
    \{\,g_{i}(u)\,\}
    &
    \text{otherwise.}
    \end{cases}
    \end{align}
    We claim that we can shrink $\tilde{U}$ 
    in such a way that each $S_{i}(u)$ is non-empty
    for $u\in \tilde{U}$.


For each $i\in\{\,1,\ldots,n\,\}$, we know by assumption on $g_0=g_0(\overline{u})$ that  $S_{i}(\overline{u})$ is non-empty, so pick $s_{i}\in S_{i}(\overline{u})$.
By choosing small enough open bisections $W_{i}\subset S
\subset {G'}
$ around $s_{i}$ and by shrinking 
the neighborhood $\tilde{U}$ of $\overline{u}$,
we get homeomorphisms $s_i (\cdot) \colon 
\tilde{U}
\to W_i$ sending $u$ to the unique element $s_i(u)\in W_i\cap G(u)\subset S(u)$;
in particular, $s_{i}(\overline{u})=s_{i}$.
Since $u\in S_0(u)$ for all $u\in \tilde{U}\subset S$, we may further let $W_0\coloneq \tilde{U}$ and let $s_0(\cdot)\colon \tilde{U}\to W_0$ be defined by $s_0(u)=u$. 


    

Since $g_{i}(u)\in G_u$ and $s_{i}(u)\in S(u)$ for each $u\in \tilde{U}$, we may
    consider the continuous map
    \[
        \kappa_i\colon \tilde{U}\to 
        G
        \quad\text{ given by }\quad
        u \mapsto
        s_{i}(u)^{-1} g_0(u)s_{i}(u) g_{i}(u)^{-1}.
    \]
    By construction of $s_{i}(\cdot)$, we have that $s_{i}(\overline{u})=s_{i}$ is an element of $S_{i}(\overline{u})$, meaning that
    \[\kappa_{i}(\overline{u})=s_{i}^{-1} g_0s_{i}g_{i}^{-1}=\overline{u}\inG^{(0)},
    \]
    so by {\'e}tale ness, $\kappa_{i}^{-1}(G^{(0)})$ is an open neighborhood of $\overline{u}$. By 
    replacing $\tilde{U}$ with its open subset $\kappa_{i}^{-1}(G^{(0)})$, 
    we can without loss of generality assume that $\kappa_{i}(\tilde{U})\subset G^{(0)}$ for all $i\in\{\,0,\ldots, n\,\}$. In other words,
    \begin{equation*}     
    s_{i}(u)^{-1} g_{0}(u) s_{i}(u)
    =
    g_{i}(u)
    \quad\text{for all } u\in \tilde{U},
    \end{equation*}
     
    as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:step2}. In particular,
    $S_{i}(u)$ is non-empty, as claimed.

\begin{figure}[h]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[height=0.6\textheight]{DWZ_step2}
    \caption{Conjugating $g_0(u)$ by $s_{i}(u)$ yields $g_i(u)$.}
    \label{fig:step2}
\end{figure}
    
    We conclude for each $i\in\{\,0,\ldots,n\,\}$ that
    \begin{align}\label{eq:sqcup V_i, finer}
    {G'}
    \supset
    \{\,
            t^{-1} g_{0}(u) t : u\in \tilde{U}, t\in S_{i}(u)
        \,\}
        \supset    
    \{\, g_{i}(u) : u\in \tilde{U}\,\}
    =
    V_{i}\cap r^{-1}(\tilde{U}).
    \end{align}
 Since $g_{i}(u)\neq g_{j}(u)$ for all $u\in \tilde{U}$ and $i\neq j$ in $\{\,0,\ldots,n\,\}$
 and since $S$ is abelian,
 it follows from $s_{i}(u)^{-1} g_{0}(u) s_{i}(u)
    =
    g_{i}(u)$
     that $g_{i}(u)\in {G'}\setminus S$, so $
     V_{i}\cap r^{-1}(\tilde{U})
     \subset \operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)\setminus S$,  and that
   \[
   |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|\geq n+1.
   \]
We have shown: for any fixed element $\overline{u}$ of $U$, we have a neighborhood $\tilde{U}\subset U$  such that 
\[
    | \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|
    \geq 
    |
   \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(\overline{u}))|
\]
for all $u\in \tilde{U}$.
Since $\overline{u}$ was arbitrary, this finishes our proof.
    \hfill\qedhere\text{ (Claim~\ref{claim:lsc})}
\end{proof}


\begin{claim}\label{claim:= n+1}
     
    There exists
    $n\geq N$
     
    and a non-empty open set $\tilde{X}\subset X$ such that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:property of tilde-X,new}
    \left|
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))
    \right|
        =
        \left| 
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)
        \right|
        = n+1
        \quad\text{for all }e\in \tilde{X}.
    \end{equation}
\end{claim}
 \begin{proof}[Proof of Claim~\ref{claim:= n+1}]
    As any $e\in X$ already satisfies the equality of set-cardinalities, it suffices to force the equality
    \[
         \left|
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))
    \right|
        = n+1.
    \]
    By lower semi-continuity (Claim~\ref{claim:lsc}), for each 
     
    $n\geq N$,
     
    the set
    \[
        C_{n} = \{ u\in U: |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|\leq n+1\}
    \]
    is closed in $U$. By our assumption on $X$ 
     
    at~\eqref{eq:new:property of X},
    we have
    \[
     U = \bigcup_{ 
        n\geq N    
    }
C_{n}.
    \]
    Since $G^{(0)}$ is locally compact, Hausdorff, and since $U$ is nonempty and open in $G^{(0)}$, it is a Baire space \cite{Kelley_book}*{34 Theorem}.  Therefore at least one of the closed sets has an interior point \cite{Schechter_book}*{20.15}. If we let $n$ be the smallest element 
     
    in $\{N,N+1,\ldots\}$
         
    for which $\operatorname{int}_{G^{(0)}}\left(C_n\right)=\operatorname{int}_{U}\left(C_n\right)$ is non-empty, then there exists
   $\overline{u}\in \operatorname{int}_{G^{(0)}}\left(C_n\right)$ with $|\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(\overline{u}))|=n+1$. By lower semi-continuity (Claim~\ref{claim:lsc}), there exists an open neighborhood $\tilde{U}\subset U$ of $\overline{u}$ such that, for all $u\in \tilde{U}$, we have
    \[
        |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|
        \geq 
        |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(\overline{u}))|
        = n+1
        .
    \]
    By definition of $C_n$, this implies that, for all $u$ in the non-empty, open set $\tilde{U}\cap \operatorname{int}_{G^{(0)}}\left(C_n\right)$, we have
    \[
        |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|
        =
        n+1
        .
    \]
    We may now let $\tilde{X}\coloneq
        r_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1} \left( \tilde{U}\cap \operatorname{int}_{G^{(0)}}\left(C_n\right)\right)
    \subset r_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}(U) = X$. 
    \hfill\qedhere\text{ (Claim~\ref{claim:= n+1})}
    \end{proof}

 
Assume now that Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:icc} fails, i.e., there exists a non-empty set $X\subset  {\mathcal{E}'}$ that is open in $\mathcal{E}$ and 
    such that Equation~\eqref{eq:new:property of X} holds for $N=1$, i.e.,     
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:property of X}
    1 < \left|
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))
    \right|
        =
        \left| 
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)
        \right|
        < \infty
        \quad\text{for all }e\in X.
    \end{equation}
    Note that~\eqref{eq:property of X} implies that $X\cap \mathcal{E}_{S}=\emptyset$, since $|\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(s)|=1$ for any $s\in S$ because $S$ is abelian. Thus, we may invoke the above claims; in particular, by
     
    replacing $X$ with its non-empty open subset $\tilde{X}$ from Claim~\ref{claim:= n+1} and by scavenging the proof of Claim~\ref{claim:lsc} (i.e., shrinking $X$ even further), we can now make the following assumptions:
\begin{itemize}
    \item The number $n\in \mathbf{Z}_{>0}$ is such that every element $e$ in the open set $\tilde{X}=X$ satisfies~\eqref{eq:property of tilde-X,new} (not just~\eqref{eq:property of X});
    \item for each $i\in\{\,0,\ldots, n\,\}$, we have pairwise disjoint
    open
    bisections $V_{i}\subset 
    \operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)\setminus S
    $
    and $W_{i}\subset S$, and homeomorphisms $g_{i}(\cdot)\colon U\coloneq r(X)\to V_{i}$  and  $s_{i}(\cdot)\colon U\to W_{i}$ 
    such that $\pi(X)=V_0$ and
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:s_i conjugate}        
    s_{i}(u)^{-1} g_{0}(u) s_{i}(u)
    =
    g_{i}(u)
    \quad\text{for all } u\in U;
    \end{equation}
    \item for $i=0$, we have $W_{0}=U$ and $s_{0}(u)=u$.
\end{itemize}
     By the property at~\eqref{eq:property of tilde-X,new} of $X=\tilde{X}$ and the fact that the $V_{i}$ are mutually disjoint, we conclude 
     from
     Equation~\eqref{eq:s_i conjugate}     that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:Ad_S g_0(u)}
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))
        = \{\, g_0(u),\ldots, g_n(u)\,\}
        \subset
        G(u)
    \end{equation}
    for all  $u\in U$.   
    This in turn implies that sets
    \begin{align}\label{eq:S_i(u), def}
    S_{i}(u)
    =
    \{\,
    t\in S(u): t^{-1} g_0(u)t=g_{i}(u)
    \,\},
    \end{align}
    which are non-empty by Equation~\eqref{eq:s_i conjugate}, are a partition of $S(u)$.
    Indeed, if $s\in S(u)$, then $s^{-1} g_0(u) s\in  \operatorname{Ad}_{S} (g_0(u))$, so  $s^{-1} g_0(u) s=g_i(u)$ for some $i\in\{\,0,\ldots,n\,\}$, meaning that $s\in S_i (u)$. Thus,
    \begin{align}\label{eq:sqcup S_i}
        S(u) = \bigsqcup_{i=0}^{n} S_{i}(u)
    \quad\text{for all } u\in U.
    \end{align}

    Next, we will deal with the $\mathcal{E}_{S}$-conjugates by `lifting' the maps $g_i(\cdot)$.
   By shrinking~$U$, we can without loss of generality assume that the bisections $V_0$ and $W_0,\ldots,W_n$ allow
   local trivializations
   of the principal $\mathbf{T}$-bundle $\mathcal{E}$, meaning that there exist  $\mathbf{T}$-equivariant homeomorphisms $\psi\colon \mathbf{T}\times V_{0} \to  \pi^{-1}(V_{0})$ 
     and, for each $i\in\{\,
     1
     ,\ldots,n\,\}$, 
     $\phi_i\colon \mathbf{T}\times W_{i}\to \pi^{-1}(W_{i})\subset \mathcal{E}_{S}$ such that the diagrams
    \begin{equation}\label{diags:psi and phi_i}
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep = small]
        \mathbf{T}\times V_{0} \ar[rr, "\psi"]\ar[rd,"\mathrm{pr}_{2}"'] && \pi^{-1}(V_{0})\ar[ld, "\pi"]
        \\
        & V_{0}
    \end{tikzcd}
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep = small]
        \mathbf{T}\times W_{i} \ar[rr, "\phi_{i}"]\ar[rd,"\mathrm{pr}_{2}"'] && \pi^{-1}(W_{i})\ar[ld, "\pi"]
        \\
        & W_{i}
    \end{tikzcd}
    \end{equation}
    commute.
    Since $W_0=U\subset G^{(0)}$,  we may choose for $i=0$ the trivialization $\phi_0\colon \mathbf{T}\times W_{0}\to \pi^{-1}(W_0)$ given by $\phi_0 (z,u)=\iota(z,u)$.
    For $i\in\{\,0,\ldots, n\,\}$,  the following maps are injective and continuous:
    \begin{align}
    \sigma_{i}(\cdot)&\colon U\to \pi^{-1} (W_{i})
    &\text{ defined by }&&\sigma_{i}(u)&\coloneq \phi_{i} (1,s_{i}(u)), \text{ and}
    \\
     e_{i}(\cdot)&\colon U \to \pi^{-1}(V_i)
    &\text{ defined by }&&
        e_{i}(u) &\coloneq \sigma_{i}(u)^{-1} \psi (1,g_{0}(u))\sigma_{i}(u).
    \end{align} 
    Since each $\sigma_i(\cdot)$ takes values in $\mathcal{E}_{S}$, the $e_{i}(u)$ are, by their very definition, $\mathcal{E}_S$-conjugates of each other. We therefore have 
     
    the following equality of sets:
     
        \begin{equation}
            \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e_i(u))=\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e_j(u)).
        \end{equation}
     For any $i$, commutativity of the diagrams at~\eqref{diags:psi and phi_i} yields that
     \begin{align*}
         \pi(e_{i}(u))
         &=
         \pi\left(
         \sigma_{i}(u)^{-1} \psi (1,g_{0}(u))\sigma_{i}(u)
         \right)
         &&\text{by definition of $e_{i}(u)$}
         \\
         &=
         \pi\left(
         \phi_{i} (1,s_{i}(u))
         \right)
         ^{-1} 
         \pi\left(\psi (1,g_{0}(u))\right)
         \pi\left(
         \phi_{i} (1,s_{i}(u))
         \right)
         &&\text{by definition of $\sigma_{i}(u)$}
         \\
         &=
         s_{i}(u)^{-1} g_0(u) s_{i}(u)
         &&\text{by~\eqref{diags:psi and phi_i}}
         \\
         &=g_{i}(u)
         &&\text{by Equation~\eqref{eq:s_i conjugate}.}
     \end{align*}
     Thus, for all $i\neq j$, it follows from $\pi(e_{i}(u))=g_{i}(u)\neq g_{j}(u)=\pi(e_{j}(u))$ that 
    $e_{i}(u)\neq e_{j}(u)$. Since~\eqref{eq:property of tilde-X,new} implies for each $u\in U$ that
    \[
    \Omega_{S}(e_{i}(u))=\Omega_{S}(e_{0}(u))
    =
    |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|
    =
    n+1,
    \]
    we conclude that 
    \begin{align}\label{eq:Ad of e_i = of e_0}
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e_i(u))=\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e_0(u))
        =
        \{\,e_{0}(u),\ldots, e_{n}(u)\,\}.
    \end{align} 

For each $i\in\{\,0,\ldots,n\,\}$, we define a $\mathbf{T}$-equivariant homeomorphism
\[
\Psi_{i}\colon \pi^{-1}(V_{i})\to \pi^{-1}(V_0)
\quad\text{ by }\quad
e\mapsto \sigma_{i}(r(e)) \, e \, \sigma_{i}(r(e))^{-1}.
\]
Note that every element $e$ of $\pi^{-1}(V_{i})$ can be written as $e=z\cdot e_{i}(u)$ for some unique $z\in\mathbf{T}$ and $u=r(e)\in r(V_{i})= U$, since $\pi(e)\in V_{i}\cap G(u)=\{\,g_{i}(u)\,\}$.
Since we assumed that $s_0(u)=u$
and $\phi_0 (z,u)=\iota(z,u)$ for all $u$ and $z\in\mathbf{T}$,
we further have that $\sigma_0(u)=
\iota(1,u) \in \mathcal{E}^{(0)}
$ for all~$u$, so that we can write $\Psi_{i}$ as follows:
\begin{align}
\Psi_{i}(z\cdot e_{i}(u))
&= 
z\cdot 
\sigma_{i}(u) e_{i}(u) \sigma_{i}(u)^{-1}
&&\text{by definition of $\Psi_{i}$}
\notag
\\&= 
z\cdot
\psi (1,g_{0}(u))
&&\text{by definition of 
$e_{i}(\cdot)$
}
\notag
\\
&=
z\cdot
\sigma_{0}(u) e_{0}(u)
\sigma_{0}(u)^{-1}
&&
\text{by definition of
$e_{0}(\cdot)$
}
\\
\label{eq:Psi_i}
&=
z\cdot e_0(u)
&&\text{ 
since $\sigma_0(u)=\iota(1,u)$.
} 
\end{align}

Now assume that $\sigma\in \mathcal{E}_{S}(u)$, so it is composable with $e=z\cdot e_i(u)\in\pi^{-1}(V_{i})$. Then it
follows from Equations~\eqref{eq:Ad of e_i = of e_0} and~\eqref{eq:Ad of ze} that
\[
    \sigma^{-1} e \sigma 
    \in
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)
    =
    \{\,z\cdot e_{0}(u),\ldots, z\cdot e_{n}(u)\,\}.
\]
On the other hand, by Equation~\eqref{eq:sqcup S_i}, we have $s_{i}(u)\pi(\sigma)\in S_{j}(u)$ for a unique $j$, so that 
\eqref{eq:S_i(u), def} implies
\begin{align*}
    \pi(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma)
    &=
    \pi(\sigma)^{-1} g_{i}(u) \pi(\sigma)
    &&\text{since $\pi(e)=\pi(e_i(u))$}
\\
    &=
    \pi(\sigma)^{-1} (s_{i}(u)^{-1} g_{0}(u) s_{i}(u)) \pi(\sigma)
    &&
    \text{by~\eqref{eq:s_i conjugate}}
    \\
    &=
    g_{j}(u)
    &&
    \text{since $s_{i}(u) \pi(\sigma)\in S_{j}(u)$ and by~\eqref{eq:s_i conjugate}}
    &&
    \\
    &=
    \pi(e_{j}(u))&&
    \text{by~\eqref{diags:psi and phi_i}}.
\end{align*}
In total, we have that
\[
    \sigma^{-1} e\sigma \in \{\,z\cdot e_{0}(u),\ldots, z\cdot e_{n}(u)\,\} \cap \mathbf{T}\cdot e_{j}(u),
\]
so $\sigma^{-1} e \sigma = z\cdot e_{j}(u)$. Hence by~\eqref{eq:Psi_i}, $\Psi_{j}(\sigma^{-1} e \sigma) = z\cdot e_{0}(u) = \Psi_{i}(e)$.
\hfill\qedhere\text{ (Lemma~\ref{lem:fancy lemma})}

label: eq:lsc inequality
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix any $\overline{u}\in U
    \subset S^{(0)}
    $ and let $g_0\coloneq g_0(\overline{u})$. 
    It will suffice to find an open neighborhood $\tilde{U}\subset U$ of $\overline u$ such that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:lsc inequality}
    | \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|
    \geq 
    |
   \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(\overline{u}))|
    \end{equation} 
for all $u\in \tilde{U}$.
 
If $|\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0)|=N+1$, then since $g_0(u)\in \pi(X)$, Inequality~\eqref{eq:lsc inequality} follows automatically from the property at~\eqref{eq:new:property of X} of $X$, and we are done; therefore, we may assume that $n\coloneq |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0)|-1 
> N\geq 0
$,
 
so that 
    \[
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0)
        =
        \{\, g_0,g_1,\ldots,g_{n}\,\}
        \subset
        G(\overline{u})
    \]
    for pairwise distinct elements $g_{i}$.
     Since $G$ is Hausdorff,
    there is an open neighborhood $\tilde{U}$ of $\overline u$
    such that there exist 
    open
    bisections 
    $V_{1},\ldots, V_{n}$ for which $g_{i}\in V_{i}$ and $\tilde{U}=s(V_{i})$  for all $i\in\{\,1,\ldots, n\,\}$. We let $g_i(\cdot)$ denote the homeomorphisms from $\tilde{U}$ to $V_i$ sending $u$ to the unique element $g_i(u)\in V_i\cap G_u$; in particular, $g_{i}(\overline{u})=g_{i}\in G(\overline{u})$.

\begin{figure}[h]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[height=0.6\textheight]{DWZ_step1}
    \caption{We shrink the open bisections ( 
     
    drawn with solid lines
     
    in color on the left) around the $S$-conjugates $g_{0},\ldots, g_{n}$ to make them disjoint and homeomorphic ( 
     
    circular neighborhoods drawn with dashed lines
     
    ).}
    \label{fig:step1}
\end{figure}



    
   

    For any two distinct $i,j\in\{\,0,\ldots,n\,\}$, we have $g_{i}(\overline{u})=g_{i}\neq g_{j}=g_{j}(\overline{u})$, so by continuity 
    we can shrink $\tilde{U}$
    and
    assume that $g_{i}(u)\neq g_{j}(u)$ for all $u\in \tilde{U}$, meaning that the bisections $V_0\cap r^{-1} (\tilde{U}),V_{1},\ldots, V_{n}$ are pairwise disjoint; see Figure~\ref{fig:step1}.
  
    For each $u\in \tilde{U}$,
    we have $s(g_0(u))=u=r(g_0(u))$, so for each $i\in\{\,0,\ldots, n\,\}$, we may 
    consider the following pairwise disjoint subsets of $S(u)$: 
    \begin{align*}
    S_{i}(u)
    =
    \{\,
    t\in S(u): t^{-1} g_0(u)t=g_{i}(u)
    \,\},
    \end{align*}
    so that
    \begin{align}        
    \{\, t^{-1} g_{0}(u) t : t\in S_{i}(u)\,\}
    =
    \begin{cases}
    \emptyset,
    &
    \text{if }S_{i}(u)=\emptyset,
    \\
    \{\,g_{i}(u)\,\}
    &
    \text{otherwise.}
    \end{cases}
    \end{align}
    We claim that we can shrink $\tilde{U}$ 
    in such a way that each $S_{i}(u)$ is non-empty
    for $u\in \tilde{U}$.


For each $i\in\{\,1,\ldots,n\,\}$, we know by assumption on $g_0=g_0(\overline{u})$ that  $S_{i}(\overline{u})$ is non-empty, so pick $s_{i}\in S_{i}(\overline{u})$.
By choosing small enough open bisections $W_{i}\subset S
\subset {G'}
$ around $s_{i}$ and by shrinking 
the neighborhood $\tilde{U}$ of $\overline{u}$,
we get homeomorphisms $s_i (\cdot) \colon 
\tilde{U}
\to W_i$ sending $u$ to the unique element $s_i(u)\in W_i\cap G(u)\subset S(u)$;
in particular, $s_{i}(\overline{u})=s_{i}$.
Since $u\in S_0(u)$ for all $u\in \tilde{U}\subset S$, we may further let $W_0\coloneq \tilde{U}$ and let $s_0(\cdot)\colon \tilde{U}\to W_0$ be defined by $s_0(u)=u$. 


    

Since $g_{i}(u)\in G_u$ and $s_{i}(u)\in S(u)$ for each $u\in \tilde{U}$, we may
    consider the continuous map
    \[
        \kappa_i\colon \tilde{U}\to 
        G
        \quad\text{ given by }\quad
        u \mapsto
        s_{i}(u)^{-1} g_0(u)s_{i}(u) g_{i}(u)^{-1}.
    \]
    By construction of $s_{i}(\cdot)$, we have that $s_{i}(\overline{u})=s_{i}$ is an element of $S_{i}(\overline{u})$, meaning that
    \[\kappa_{i}(\overline{u})=s_{i}^{-1} g_0s_{i}g_{i}^{-1}=\overline{u}\inG^{(0)},
    \]
    so by {\'e}tale ness, $\kappa_{i}^{-1}(G^{(0)})$ is an open neighborhood of $\overline{u}$. By 
    replacing $\tilde{U}$ with its open subset $\kappa_{i}^{-1}(G^{(0)})$, 
    we can without loss of generality assume that $\kappa_{i}(\tilde{U})\subset G^{(0)}$ for all $i\in\{\,0,\ldots, n\,\}$. In other words,
    \begin{equation*}     
    s_{i}(u)^{-1} g_{0}(u) s_{i}(u)
    =
    g_{i}(u)
    \quad\text{for all } u\in \tilde{U},
    \end{equation*}
     
    as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:step2}. In particular,
    $S_{i}(u)$ is non-empty, as claimed.

\begin{figure}[h]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[height=0.6\textheight]{DWZ_step2}
    \caption{Conjugating $g_0(u)$ by $s_{i}(u)$ yields $g_i(u)$.}
    \label{fig:step2}
\end{figure}
    
    We conclude for each $i\in\{\,0,\ldots,n\,\}$ that
    \begin{align}\label{eq:sqcup V_i, finer}
    {G'}
    \supset
    \{\,
            t^{-1} g_{0}(u) t : u\in \tilde{U}, t\in S_{i}(u)
        \,\}
        \supset    
    \{\, g_{i}(u) : u\in \tilde{U}\,\}
    =
    V_{i}\cap r^{-1}(\tilde{U}).
    \end{align}
 Since $g_{i}(u)\neq g_{j}(u)$ for all $u\in \tilde{U}$ and $i\neq j$ in $\{\,0,\ldots,n\,\}$
 and since $S$ is abelian,
 it follows from $s_{i}(u)^{-1} g_{0}(u) s_{i}(u)
    =
    g_{i}(u)$
     that $g_{i}(u)\in {G'}\setminus S$, so $
     V_{i}\cap r^{-1}(\tilde{U})
     \subset \operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)\setminus S$,  and that
   \[
   |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|\geq n+1.
   \]
We have shown: for any fixed element $\overline{u}$ of $U$, we have a neighborhood $\tilde{U}\subset U$  such that 
\[
    | \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|
    \geq 
    |
   \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(\overline{u}))|
\]
for all $u\in \tilde{U}$.
Since $\overline{u}$ was arbitrary, this finishes our proof.
    \hfill\qedhere\text{ (Claim~\ref{claim:lsc})}

title: Claim
body_md:
\label{claim:= n+1}
     
    There exists
    $n\geq N$
     
    and a non-empty open set $\tilde{X}\subset X$ such that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:property of tilde-X,new}
    \left|
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))
    \right|
        =
        \left| 
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)
        \right|
        = n+1
        \quad\text{for all }e\in \tilde{X}.
    \end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As any $e\in X$ already satisfies the equality of set-cardinalities, it suffices to force the equality
    \[
         \left|
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))
    \right|
        = n+1.
    \]
    By lower semi-continuity (Claim~\ref{claim:lsc}), for each 
     
    $n\geq N$,
     
    the set
    \[
        C_{n} = \{ u\in U: |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|\leq n+1\}
    \]
    is closed in $U$. By our assumption on $X$ 
     
    at~\eqref{eq:new:property of X},
    we have
    \[
     U = \bigcup_{ 
        n\geq N    
    }
C_{n}.
    \]
    Since $G^{(0)}$ is locally compact, Hausdorff, and since $U$ is nonempty and open in $G^{(0)}$, it is a Baire space \cite{Kelley_book}*{34 Theorem}.  Therefore at least one of the closed sets has an interior point \cite{Schechter_book}*{20.15}. If we let $n$ be the smallest element 
     
    in $\{N,N+1,\ldots\}$
         
    for which $\operatorname{int}_{G^{(0)}}\left(C_n\right)=\operatorname{int}_{U}\left(C_n\right)$ is non-empty, then there exists
   $\overline{u}\in \operatorname{int}_{G^{(0)}}\left(C_n\right)$ with $|\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(\overline{u}))|=n+1$. By lower semi-continuity (Claim~\ref{claim:lsc}), there exists an open neighborhood $\tilde{U}\subset U$ of $\overline{u}$ such that, for all $u\in \tilde{U}$, we have
    \[
        |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|
        \geq 
        |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(\overline{u}))|
        = n+1
        .
    \]
    By definition of $C_n$, this implies that, for all $u$ in the non-empty, open set $\tilde{U}\cap \operatorname{int}_{G^{(0)}}\left(C_n\right)$, we have
    \[
        |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g_0(u))|
        =
        n+1
        .
    \]
    We may now let $\tilde{X}\coloneq
        r_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1} \left( \tilde{U}\cap \operatorname{int}_{G^{(0)}}\left(C_n\right)\right)
    \subset r_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}(U) = X$. 
    \hfill\qedhere\text{ (Claim~\ref{claim:= n+1})}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:phew}
    Assume that $S\subset {G'}$
   is abelian, and that $X$ is a non-empty open subset of ${\mathcal{E}'}$ with $X\cap \mathcal{E}_{S}=\emptyset$. If there exists $N\in\{0,1,\ldots\}$ such that
    \begin{align}\notag
    N < \left|
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))
    \right|
        &=
        \left| 
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)
        \right|
        < \infty
        &\text{for all }e\in X,
    \intertext{
    then there exists
    $n\geq N$
    and a non-empty open set $\tilde{X}\subset X$ such that}   
    n+1
    =
    \left|
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))
    \right|
        &=
        \left| 
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)
        \right|
        &\text{for all }e\in \tilde{X}.
    \end{align}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have already seen in Corollary~\ref{cor:S max in terms of Omega} that \ref{it:prop:max:S_April23} and \ref{it:prop:max:S in terms of Omega + maximal} are equivalent, and in Example~\ref{ex-abelian} that $\mathcal{E}_{S}$ is abelian  if and only if $B\coloneq i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r} (S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))$ is abelian.
In particular, we can assume that $\mathcal{E}_{S}$ is an abelian  subset of $ {\mathcal{E}'}$, and we only have to check that maximality of $B$ is equivalent to 
 
  the two conditions
   
        \@ifundefined{repeatable@both-conditions}{NOT FOUND}{\@nameuse{repeatable@both-conditions}} 
     
 

 
  $\lnot$\ref{it:prop:max_new:B}$\implies\lnot$\ref{it:prop:max:S_April23}: 
  Suppose $B$ is not maximal abelian in $A\coloneq \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r} (G;\mathcal{E})$, meaning there exists $a\in A\setminus B$ such that $ab = ba$ for all $b\in B$. Let $h\coloneq j_{G}(a)$.
  Since $a\notin B$ and since $S$ is closed in $G$, Proposition~\ref{prop:support in S} asserts that 
  $\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(h)\not\subset \mathcal{E}_{S}$.
  
To show $\lnot$\ref{it:prop:max:S_April23}, we may assume that $S$ satisfies Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:Int Omega=1}; we claim that Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:icc} fails because of 
 
(an open subset of) 
 
the set $X\coloneq \operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(h)\cap \mathcal{E}\setminus\mathcal{E}_{S}$.
Since $S$ is closed, $X$ is an open subset of $\mathcal{E}$, and by the first paragraph, $X$ is non-empty. 

By Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:Int Omega=1}, we have $G^{(0)}\subset S$; in particular,
since $a$ commutes with $B$ and $G^{(0)}\subset S$, $a$ commutes with $C_0(G^{(0)})$, so \cite{ren:irms08}*{Theorem 4.2(a)} implies that $\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(h)\subset  {\mathcal{E}'}$, so $X\subset {\mathcal{E}'}$. We thus may evaluate $\Omega_{S}$ at elements of $X$.


We claim that $\Omega_{S}$ does not take on the value $\infty$ on $X$.
 
Fix $e\in X$; we will first prove that $\pi$ is injective on $\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)$.
  If $\sigma\in\mathcal{E}_{S}(r(e))$ is such that $\pi(\sigma^{-1} e \sigma)=\pi(e)$, then there exists $z\in\mathbf{T}$ such that $\sigma^{-1} e \sigma = z\cdot e$. Using the assumption that $a$ commutes with every element of $B$, Lemma~\ref{lem:conjugation equality} 
  and $\mathbf{T}$-equivariance of $h=j_{G}(a)$ imply that
  \begin{equation}
      h(e) \overset{\text{L.~\ref{lem:conjugation
      equality}}}{=} h(\sigma^{-1} e \sigma) = h(z\cdot e) = zh(e).
  \end{equation}
   As
  $e\in X$, we have
  $h(e)\neq 0$, so the above
  implies $z=1$, so $\sigma^{-1} e\sigma=  e$. Thus,
  $\pi$ is injective on $\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)$. 
  
  To conclude that $\Omega_{S}(e)$ is finite, it remains to show that $|\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))|<\infty$.
  Because $h \in C_0 (G;\mathcal{E})$,
  we may find a compact $K\subset  G$ such that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:h(e')_new}
    |h  (e')|
    < |h  (e)|
    \text{ for all }e'\in \pi^{-1}(G\setminus K).
    \end{equation}
    We claim that $I\coloneq \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))$ is contained in the compact set $K$. Indeed, if $e'\in \pi^{-1}(I)$, then
    $e'=z\cdot \sigma e \sigma^{-1}$ for some $z\in\mathbf{T}$ and some
    $\sigma\in \mathcal{E}_{S}$, and so
    \[
        |h (e')|
        =
        |z\, h (\sigma e \sigma^{-1})|
        =
        |h (\sigma e \sigma^{-1})|\overset{\text{L.~\ref{lem:conjugation
      equality}}}{=}|h (e)|.
    \]
    Combined with Equation~\eqref{eq:h(e')_new}, this shows
    that
    $\pi^{-1}(I)\subset  \mathcal{E}\setminus\pi^{-1}(G\setminus K) =
    \pi^{-1}(K)$. In other words, $I=\pi(\pi^{-1}(I))$ is contained in
    the compact set $K$. Since $I$ is also a subset of the discrete
    set $G(r(e))$, $I$ is finite,     
    as claimed.
  
    Since $G^{(0)}\subset S$ furthermore implies that $\Omega_{S}(e)>0$ for all $e\in{\mathcal{E}'}$, we have shown all in all that
    \begin{align}
    0 < \left|
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))
    \right|
        &=
        \left| 
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)
        \right|
        < \infty
        &\text{for all }e\in X.
    \intertext{By Lemma~\ref{lem:phew}, there thus exists
    $n\geq 0$
    and a non-empty open set $\tilde{X}\subset X$ such that}   
    n+1
    =
    \left|
    \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(\pi(e))
    \right|
        &=
        \left| 
        \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(e)
        \right|
        &\text{for all }e\in \tilde{X}.
    \end{align}
    Note that $n$ must be larger than $0$: otherwise, $\tilde{X}$ would be contained in $\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{E}}\left(\Omega_{S}^{-1} (\{\,1\,\})\right)$, which by Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:Int Omega=1} coincides with $\mathcal{E}_{S} \subset \mathcal{E}\setminus X$. In other words, we have
    \[
    \tilde{X}
    \subset 
    \Omega_{S}^{-1} (\mathbf{Z}_{>1}).
    \]
    Since $\tilde{X}$ is open and non-empty, this shows that Condition~\eqref {eq:thm:May17:icc} fails.
    

\smallskip


$\lnot$\ref{it:prop:max:S_April23}$\implies\lnot$\ref{it:prop:max_new:B}:
Assume first that 
Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:Int Omega=1} fails. By Corollary~\ref{cor:S max in terms of Omega}, this means that there exists an open subgroupoid $T$ of $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ whose twist $\mathcal{E}_{T}$ is abelian and such that $S\subsetneq T$. 
We have by Proposition~\ref{prop:support in S} that
\[
B=i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))
\subset
\{\,a\in \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E}) : \operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(j_{G}(a))\subset \mathcal{E}_{S}\,\}.
\]
In particular, $i(C_c(T;\mathcal{E}_{T}))\not\subset B$, so $B$
is a proper subalgebra of the commutative $i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(T;\mathcal{E}_{T}))$ and $B$ is hence not maximal abelian.

    Now assume that Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:icc} fails. Let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{>0}$, $V_0,\ldots,V_n$, and $\Psi_{0},\ldots, \Psi_{n}$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:fancy lemma}.
    Fix $e_{0}\in \pi^{-1}(V_0)$ and some precompact open $V$ around $\pi(e_0)$ such that $V\subset\overline{V}\subset V_{0}$. Pick an $h_{0}\in C_c(G;\mathcal{E})$ with $\pi(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(h_0))\subset V$ and such that $h_{0}(z\cdot e_0)=z$ for all $z\in \mathbf{T}$. For each $1\leq i\leq n$, define at $e\in \mathcal{E}$
    \[
        h_{i}(e)    
        =
        \begin{cases}
            h_{0} (\Psi_{i}(e)),
            &
            \text{if }e\in \pi^{-1}(V_{i}),
            \\
            0, & \text{otherwise}.
        \end{cases}
    \]
    By assumption on the support of $h_{0}$, this is continuous and compactly supported, and since $\Psi_i$ and $h_{0}$ are $\mathbf{T}$-equivariant, so is $h_{i}$. In other words, $h_{i}\in C_{c}(G;\mathcal{E})$.

    Let $h\coloneq \sum_{i=0}^{n} h_{i}\in C_c(G;\mathcal{E})$. Since the $V_{i}$'s are mutually disjoint, so are the $\pi^{-1}(V_{i})$'s. In particular $\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(h)=\bigsqcup_{i=0}^{n}\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(h_{i})$, which contains the point $e_{0}\in \pi^{-1}(V_{0})\subset  \mathcal{E}\setminus \mathcal{E}_{S}$. 
    By Proposition~\ref{prop:support in S}, this means 
that $h\notin B$.     
    We claim that $h$ commutes with $B$, proving that $B$ is  not maximal abelian, as desired.

     
    Since $\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(h)\subset \bigsqcup_{i=0}^{n}\pi^{-1}(V_i)$ and since $V_i\subset {G'}$ by construction (Lemma~\ref{lem:fancy lemma}), we have $\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(h)\subset {\mathcal{E}'}$. Thus, according 
    to Lemma~\ref{lem:conjugation equality}, it suffices to show that, for any $u\inG^{(0)}$,
     $e\in\mathcal{E}(u)$, and $\sigma\in\mathcal{E}_{S}(u)$, we have $h(e)=h(\sigma^{-1} e \sigma)$. If $h(e)\neq 0$, then there exists a unique $i\in\{\,0,\ldots,n\,\}$ such that $e\in \pi^{-1}(V_i)$.
    By construction of the maps $\Psi_{0},\ldots,\Psi_{n}$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:fancy lemma}, there exists a unique $j\in\{\,0,\ldots, n\,\}$ such that $\sigma^{-1} e\sigma\in\pi^{-1}(V_{j})$, and we have $\Psi_{j}(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma)=\Psi_{i}(e)$. By definition of $h$, we conclude
    \[
    h(e)=h_0 (\Psi_i(e)) = h_0 (\Psi_j(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma)) = h(\sigma^{-1} e\sigma),
    \]
    as needed. Replacing $e$ with $\sigma e\sigma^{-1}$ in this argument proves that indeed, $h(e)=h(\sigma^{-1} e \sigma)$ for all $\sigma$.

label: cor:Breg
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:Breg}
  If $i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))$ is regular in $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$, then the following statements are equivalent.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
      
    \item\label{it:cor:Breg:B} $i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))$ is a Cartan subalgebra of $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$.
    \item\label{it:cor:Breg:S:Omega} $S$ satisfies Conditions~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:Int Omega=1} and~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:icc}, and $S$ is closed in $G$.\item\label{it:cor:Breg:S:Omega+max} $S$ is maximal among open subgroupoids of $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ for which
      $\mathcal{E}_{S}$ is abelian, satisfies Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:icc}, and $S$ is closed in $G$.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $B\coloneq i (\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))$ and $A\coloneq \ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G;\mathcal{E})$.
   
   
    
    \ref{it:cor:Breg:B}$\implies$\ref{it:cor:Breg:S:Omega+max}:  
     
    Since $B$ is maximal abelian and since $i (\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))\subset i (\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(T;\mathcal{E}_{T}))$ for any intermediate open subgroupoid $S\subset T\subset G$, it follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:S max in terms of Omega}, \ref{item:cor:S max implies}$\implies$\ref{item:cor:S max implied by}, that $S^{(0)}=G^{(0)}$. Thus, the
     
    existence of a conditional expectation $A\to B$ implies by \cite{BEFPR:2021:Intermediate}*{Lemma 3.4} that $S$ is closed
   in $G$.  Since $S$ is clopen in $G$ and $B$ is a Cartan subalgebra of $A$,
   it follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:max_new}, \ref{it:prop:max_new:B}$\implies$\ref{it:prop:max:S in terms of Omega + maximal},  that $S$ satisfies the remaining claimed properties.

   
   \ref{it:cor:Breg:S:Omega+max}$\implies$\ref{it:cor:Breg:B}:

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Bisections are normalisers}
  Assume that $S\subset {G'}$ is normal 
  in $G$
  and that
  $ h \in C_c(G; \mathcal{E})$ has support equal to the preimage under $\pi$ of
  a bisection. Then 
  $ h * f * h^{*} \in i (C_c(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))$ for all
  $ f \in i (C_c(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))$.

label:
Bisections are normalisers
      Equation 1
title: Proof
body_md:
The argument is essentially
unchanged from \cite{DGNRW:Cartan}*{Lemma 3.11}, one just has to account for the twist.
  Because $C_c(G;\mathcal{E})$ is closed under convolution, it suffices to show
  that $ h * f * h^{*} $ is supported on $\mathcal{E}_S$.  For $e\in \mathcal{E}$, we
  have
  \begin{align*}
    h   *    f   *   h^{*} (e)
    &=
      \sum_{\pi(e_{1}) \in G^{s(e)}} \sum_{\pi(e_{2}) \in G_{s(e_1)}}
      h(e e_{1}e_{2}^{-1}) \, f (e_{2})  
      \,  \overline{h (e_{1})}.
      \label{Bisections are normalisers
      Equation 1}  
  \end{align*}
  Assume $e\in\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(h * f * h^{*} )$. Since $f$ is supported on
  $\mathcal{E}_S$, there exist $e_{1}\in \mathcal{E}^{s(e)}$ and
  $e_{2}\in (\mathcal{E}_{S})_{s(e_{1})}$ such that
  $ee_{1}e_{2}^{-1}, e_{1}\in \operatorname{supp}^{\circ} (h)$. Since $S\subset {G'}$,
  the unit $r(e_{2})=s(ee_{1}e_{2}^{-1})$ coincides with
  $s(e_{2})=s(e_{1})$. Since $ee_{1}e_{2}^{-1}$ and $e_{1}$ 
  therefore
  have the
  same source, our assumption on the support of $h$ implies that
  $ee_{1}e_{2}^{-1}=z\cdot e_{1}$ for some $z\in\mathbf{T} $. Thus, $e=e_{1}(z\cdot e_{2})e_{1}^{-1}$
  is an element of $\mathcal{E}_{S}$
  by normality of~$S$, as claimed.

body_md:
\label{cor:regular if normal}
  Assume $S\subset {G'}$.  If $S$ is normal in $G$, then
  \[ 
        \{\,
        a\in C_{c}(G;\mathcal{E}):
        \pi(\operatorname{supp}^{\circ}(a)) \text{ is a bisection}
        \,\} 
        \subset 
        N(i (\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))),
    \]
    so $ i (\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S;\mathcal{E}_{S}))$ is regular.

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{it:thm:May17:B:subset}$\implies$\ref{it:thm:May17:B:cap}:

body_md: Consider $G= \mathfrak{S}_{3}$, the symmetric group on $3$ elements. Its (untwisted, reduced) group $\ensuremath{C^{*}}$-algebra $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}( \mathfrak{S}_{3})$ must be non-commutative and, as a vector space, be of dimension $6$. In other words, we must have $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}( \mathfrak{S}_{3}) = \mathbf{C}  \oplus M_2(\mathbf{C}) \oplus \mathbf{C}$. If $D_{2}$ denotes the diagonal subalgebra of $M_{2}(\mathbf{C})$, then $\mathbf{C} \oplus D_{2}\oplus\mathbf{C}$ is a Cartan subalgebra of $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}( \mathfrak{S}_{3})$ (actually, it is a $\ensuremath{C^{*}}$-diagonal). However, by Lagrange's theorem, no subgroup of $ \mathfrak{S}_{3}$ is of order $4$, so this Cartan subalgebra cannot have arisen as $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S)$ for $S\leq  \mathfrak{S}_{3}$.
