title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:immcentr is bad}
    Let $\mathfrak{S}_3$ denote the symmetric group of degree $3$ and let $\mathfrak{A}_3$ denote the alternating group, a normal abelian subgroup of $\mathfrak{S}_3$. In $\prod_{n\in  \mathbf{N} } \mathfrak{S}_{3}$, consider the element $h$ that has the transposition $(12)$ in each coordinate. In $\oplus_{n\in  \mathbf{N} } \mathfrak{A}_{3}$, consider for each $k\in\mathbf{N}$, the element $s_k$ that has $(123)$ in the $k$-coordinate and the identity element everywhere else. Since  $(123)^{-1} (12)(123)=(13)$, we see that
    \(
    s_k^{-1} h s_{k}
    \)
    has the entry $(13)$ in the $k$-component and $(12)$ everywhere else; in particular, $h$ does not commute with $s_{k}$. Consider the following subgroups of $\prod_{n\in  \mathbf{N} } \mathfrak{S}_{3}$:
    \[
        S\coloneq \langle s_{k} : k \in \mathbf{N}\rangle 
        \leq
        G\coloneq
        \langle S,h\rangle.
    \]
    A quick computation shows that $S=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf{N}} \mathfrak{A}_{3}$; by construction, $S$ is maximal abelian in $G$. Note that $S$ is normal in $G$ since $\mathfrak{A}_{3}$ is normal in $\mathfrak{S}_{3}$.
    We claim that $S\leq G$ satisfies~\eqref{eq:icc}. 

    Assume that $g\in G\setminus S$; it suffices to prove that the set of~$S$-conjugates of $g$ is infinite. Since $S$ is normal and $h^2=e$, we can write $g=h^{i}s$ for some exponent $i\in \{0,1\}$ and some element $s\in S$. Since $g\notin S$, we must have $i=1$. Since all but finitely components of~$S$ are trivial, we see that all but finitely components of $g$ are given by the transposition $(12)$. The same computation as that done for $h$ then shows that the set $\{\,s_{k}^{-1} g s_{k}:k\in\mathbf{N}\,\}$ is infinite. This finishes our proof that~\eqref{eq:icc} is satisfied. Thus, by Corollary~\ref{cor:formerly thm:main}, we conclude that $i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_r(S))$ is a Cartan subalgebra of $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G)$.

    In Remark~\ref{rmk:icc vs immcentr}, we have shown that Assumption~\eqref{eq:immcentr} implies Assumption~\eqref{eq:icc}. The example here shows that the converse is false: since the two non-trivial elements of the alternating group $\mathfrak{A}_3$ are of order $3$, any non-trivial element of~$S$ is of order $3$, so that $gs^{3}=g=s^{3}g$ for any  $s\in S$ and any $g\in G$ (i.e., the hypothesis in~\eqref{eq:immcentr} is satisfied for $k=3$ and every $g\in G$), despite not every element of $G$ commuting with every element of~$S$ (i.e., the conclusion of~\eqref{eq:immcentr} is not satisfied for $k=3$). In particular,  \cite{DGNRW:Cartan}*{Theorem 3.1} and \cite{BG:2023:Gamma-Cartan-pp}*{Proposition 3.4} do not see that $i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S))$ is a Cartan subalgebra of $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G)$.

\label{cor:BNRWS}
    Assume that $G$ is a  locally compact, Hausdorff, {\'e}tale\ groupoid, and suppose that $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ is abelian. 
    Then
    $i(\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)))$ is a Cartan subalgebra if and only if  $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ is closed in~$G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $S\coloneq \operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ is abelian, any $g\in \operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ satisfies
   \[
   \operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g)=\{\,t^{-1} g t:t\in \operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)\,\} = \{\,g\,\}
   ,\]
   so that
   \[
    X\coloneq
    \Bigl\{
    g\in {G'}: 1< |\operatorname{Ad}_{S}(g)|<\infty
    \Bigr\}
    \subset 
    {G'}\setminus \operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)
    .
  \]
  In other words, $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left(X\right)=\emptyset$ and so Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:icc} is satisfied. 
  Since $\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ is normal in $G$, it 
  follows from 
Corollary~\ref{cor:Breg} (in tandem with Corollary~\ref{cor:regular if normal})
  that it is a Cartan subalgebra if and only if $S=\operatorname{int}_{G}\left({G'}\right)$ is closed.

title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:rotation}
  On $G=\mathbf{Z}^2$, consider the $2$-cocycle
  $\mathbf{c}_{\theta}\colon G^2\to \mathbf{T}$ defined for a fixed $\theta\in(0,1)$ by
    \[
        \mathbf{c}_{\theta} ((m_{1},m_{2}),(n_{1},n_{2}))=e^{2\pi i
          \theta m_{2}n_{1}}. 
    \]
    Since $G$ is  a discrete abelian group,
    every subgroup is clopen and normal, so that
    Corollary~\ref{cor:Breg} (in tandem with Corollary~\ref{cor:regular if normal} and with Remark~\ref{rmk:cocycle symmetric})
    states that
    a subgroup $S$ of $G$  will give rise to a Cartan subalgebra
      $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S,\mathbf{c}_{\theta}|_{{S^2}})$ of
      $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G,\mathbf{c}_{\theta})$ if and only if 
    $S$ 
    is maximal subject to the condition that
      $c|_{{S^2}}$ is symmetric.  Let us describe these
      maximal subgroups.  Note first that every $S\leq G$ can be
    written as $\mathbf{Z}\cdot (k,0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot (m,n)$, where either
    $k\ge0$ and $m=n=0$, or $k=0$ and $n>0$, or $k>0$, $n>0$ and
    $m\ge0$.
    
  If $\theta\notin \mathbf{Q}$, then $\mathbf{Z}\cdot (k,0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot (m,n)$ with
  $k,n>0$ does not give rise to a Cartan subalgebra, since its
  $2$-cocycle is not symmetric and hence its \ensuremath{C^{*}}-algebra not
  abelian.
  If $kn=0$, then the remaining subgroups are of the
    form, $\mathbf{Z}\cdot (m,n)$, and give rise to a regular abelian
    subalgebra of $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_r(G,\mathbf{c}_{\theta})$.  However, only
    $\mathbf{Z}\cdot (1,0)$, $\mathbf{Z}\cdot (0,1)$, and $\mathbf{Z}\cdot (m,n)$ with
    $\gcd(m,n)=1$ are \emph{maximal} with symmetric $2$-cocycle.
    (The
  latter subgroups were forgotten in \cite{MFO2022}*{p.\ 2099, Example 1}.)

    
    This leaves 
    the 
    case that
    $\theta = p/q \in \mathbf{Q}$. If $p=0$,
    then $G$ itself is 
    maximal. If $p\neq 0$, we may assume $\gcd(p,q)=1$. 

    \begin{claim*}
      $\mathbf{Z}\cdot (k,0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot (m,n)$ is maximal among
    subgroups on which the $2$-cocycle  
        $c_{p/q}$ 
    is symmetric if and only if
    $nk=q$. 
    \end{claim*}
      

    \begin{proof}[Proof of Claim.]
      It is easy to check that the $2$-cocycle restricted to
      $\mathbf{Z}\cdot (k,0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot (m,n)$ is symmetric if and only if
      either $k=0$ or $q\mid nk$. In particular, no subgroup of the
      form $\mathbf{Z}\cdot(m,n)$ 
      with $n >0$
      can give rise to a Cartan
      subalgebra, as it as properly contained in, for example,
      $\mathbf{Z}\cdot(q,0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot(m,n)$ and hence not
      maximal.
      Similarly, if $k>0$, then $\mathbf{Z}\cdot (k,0)\subset
        \mathbf{Z}\cdot (1,0) \oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot (0,q)$.
        So let
      us focus on the subgroups $\mathbf{Z}\cdot(k,0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot(m,n)$ with
      $kn > 0$ and $q\mid nk$.

        Note first that $H=\mathbf{Z}\cdot(k,0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot(m,n)$ is a subgroup of
        $K=\mathbf{Z}\cdot(k',0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot(m',n')$ if and only if 
    \begin{align}\label{eq:H subgp iff}
        k'\mid k, 
        \quad 
        n'\mid n,
        \quad
        \text{and}
        \quad
        k'n'\mid (mn' - nm').
    \end{align}
    In particular, if $nk=q$ and $m$ is arbitrary, then $H$ is
    maximal: if $H\leq K$ {\em and} $\mathbf{c}_{p/q}$ is symmetric
    on~$K$, then the first two conditions of~\eqref{eq:H subgp iff}
    imply that $n'=n$ and $k'=k$, and the last condition boils down to
    $k\mid (m-m')$, which is symmetric in $m$ and $m'$, forcing
    $H= K$.

    So assume now that $q\mid nk$ but $q<nk$; we must show that $H$ is not
    maximal.
    
    If $k\mathbin{\nmid } q$, then there exists $k'\mid k$, $k'\neq k$,
    such that $q\mid nk'$, so that $\mathbf{c}_{p/q}$ is symmetric on
    $\mathbf{Z}\cdot(k',0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot(m,n)$ which, by~\eqref{eq:H subgp iff} and
    since $k\neq k'$, properly contains $H$. We can thus assume that
    $q=kn'$ for some $n'\in\mathbf{N} $; note that $q\mid nk$ then means $n'\mid n$,
    and $q< nk$ means $n'< n$.

    
    If $\gcd(n/n', k)=l > 1$, then $\mathbf{Z}\cdot(k/l,0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot(m,n)$ properly
    contains $H$. Since $n'l$ divides $n$ by choice of $l$, we see
    that $q=n'k=(n'l)(k/l)$ divides $n(k/l)$, so that the $2$-cocycle
    is symmetric on this supergroup of $H$, proving that $H$ is not
    maximal. We can thus assume that $\gcd(n/n',k)=1$.
    
    By Bezout's identity, there exist $b,c\in \mathbf{Z}$ with $ (n/n')b +
    kc=1$. Multiplying both sides by $n'm$, we  conclude 
    \[
        n'k \mid  (mn' - n(bm)).
    \]
    Together with $n'\mid n$, this implies by~\eqref{eq:H subgp iff} that
    $H\leq \mathbf{Z}\cdot(k,0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot(bm,n')$ and that, 
    as $n'\neq n$, this
    containment is proper. As $kn'=q$, the $2$-cocycle is symmetric on
    this supergroup, proving that $H$ is not maximal.
  \end{proof}
  
    To sum up: 
    if $\gcd(p,q)=1$, a subgroup $H=\mathbf{Z}\cdot(k,0)\oplus \mathbf{Z}\cdot(m,n)$ of $\mathbf{Z}^2$ 
    gives rise to a Cartan subalgebra of $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_r(G,\mathbf{c}_{p/q})$ if and only if $q=nk$.

body_md:
The example here is a slight simplification of the one given in
  \cite{DGNRW:Cartan}*{Section~7}.
  Consider the set
  $G=\mathbf{Z} /4\mathbf{Z} \times \mathbf{Z} \times\mathbf{Z} $ with the discrete topology. We make
  it a non-abelian group with $2$-cocycle ${c}$ by defining
  \[
    (x,y,z)\cdot (m,n,k)=(x+m+2zn, y+n, z+k) \quad\text{and}\quad
    {c}((m,n,k),(m',n',k'))=(-1)^{nm'}.
  \]
  We will show that $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(G,{c})$ does not have a Cartan subalgebra that comes from a subgroupoid.
  
  
  The maximal abelian subgroups on which ${c}$ is symmetric (i.e.,
  for which the twist is abelian) are
  \[
    S_{1} \coloneq \mathbf{Z} /4\mathbf{Z} \times 2\mathbf{Z} \times \mathbf{Z} \quad\text{and}\quad
    S_{2} \coloneq 2\mathbf{Z} /4\mathbf{Z} \times \mathbf{Z} \times 2\mathbf{Z} .
  \]
  For trivial reasons, these are clopen and have full unit
  space, and since
\begin{align*}
        (m,n,k)\cdot 
        (x,y,z)\cdot 
        (m,n,k)^{-1}
    &=
    (x+2(ky-zn), y, z),
\end{align*}
we see that both subgroups are normal and that
\[
  \{\, s\cdot (0,1,1)\cdot s^{-1} \mid s\in S_{i} \,\} = \{\, (0,1,1),
    (2, 1, 1) \,\} .
\] 
Thus, 
\[
 \Omega_{S_{i}}\bigl((0,1,1)\bigr)=|\operatorname{Ad}_{S_{i}}\bigl((0,1,1)\bigr)|=2,
\]
so
\[
 (0,1,1)\in \Omega_{S_{i}}^{-1}(\mathbf{Z}_{>1}).
\]
In other words, the two maximal subgroups of~$G$ with abelian twist do
not satisfy Condition~\eqref{eq:thm:May17:icc}. Thus, 
Corollary~\ref{cor:Breg}
yields that $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S_{1}) $ and $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S_{2}) $ are not Cartan subalgebras. And indeed,
$\delta_{(0,1,1)} + \delta_{(2,1,1)}$ commutes with the
\ensuremath{C^{*}}-algebras 
$\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S_{i})$ while not being contained in them,
proving that $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S_{1}) $ and $\ensuremath{C^{*}}_{r}(S_{2}) $ are not maximal abelian.
